title: Infectious and non-infectious diseases: how they differ, how they spread and how to prevent them

summary.text: You can sit beside a grandmother with diabetes, but you are kept away from a cousin with chickenpox. Why? In this unit you will list illnesses in your own family, mark ill houses on two maps with dice to see which illness is catching, and play a card game on how germs travel.
summary.art: A grandmother and a girl of ten sitting close together on a sofa, and through a doorway a boy with chickenpox spots resting alone in bed.

intro.hook: You may sit beside a grandmother who has diabetes all day. But you are kept away from a cousin who has chickenpox. Both are ill. Why is one illness passed on and the other not? And how did anyone find out which is which?
intro.text: Some diseases are caused by germs, and many of those pass from one person to the next. They are called infectious diseases. Colds, chickenpox, cholera, malaria and tuberculosis are infectious. Other diseases have no germ behind them, and nobody catches them. They are called non-infectious diseases. Diabetes, asthma, heart disease and most cancers are non-infectious. In this unit you find out how people tell the two kinds apart. You make two maps of 36 houses with dice, one for an illness that is catching and one for an illness that is not. You roll dice for two groups of 30 people to see what a risk does. You fill bottles with smoke to find out how fresh air clears a room. By the end you can name the road each common germ travels and the protection that blocks that road. You can also say what raises the chance of a heart attack, a stroke, diabetes and cancer.
intro.art: Two sheets of squared paper side by side on a table, one with ill houses in a tight cluster and one with ill houses scattered, with a die between them.

outcomes: By the end I can say what infectious and non-infectious diseases are, and sort common diseases into the two groups.
By the end I can name the five roads germs travel, with the symptoms of one disease for each road.
By the end I can match each protection to the road or the cause that the protection blocks.
By the end I can explain what causes heart attack, stroke, diabetes and cancer, and what a risk factor is.
By the end I can use a map, a day chart or two groups to work out what kind of illness I am looking at.
By the end I can say how HIV does and does not spread, and why nobody should be kept away for an illness that is not catching.
By the end I can say what scientists still argue about, such as germs behind diseases that were called non-infectious.

terms.meaning: A condition in which part of the body, or the mind, does not work as it should, for some time.
terms.example: A cold, malaria, diabetes and asthma are all diseases. A cut finger is an injury, which is different.
terms.art: Four small pictures in a row: a child sneezing, a person shivering under a blanket, a finger-prick blood test and an inhaler.

terms.meaning: A microbe who can make a person ill. A microbe is a living being too small to see. Germs can be bacteria, viruses, fungi or tiny parasites.
terms.example: The cholera germ is a bacterium. The measles germ is a virus. The malaria germ is a tiny parasite.
terms.art: Three circles like views in a microscope, showing comma-shaped bacteria, a round spiky virus and a ring-shaped parasite inside a red blood cell.

terms.meaning: A disease caused by a germ who gets into the body and multiplies there.
terms.example: Typhoid, dengue, tuberculosis and chickenpox are infectious diseases.
terms.art: An outline of a child with a few small dots entering at the nose and many more dots inside the chest.

terms.meaning: A disease that no germ causes. Nobody catches it from another person.
terms.example: Diabetes, asthma, anaemia, heart disease and most cancers are non-infectious diseases.
terms.art: A grandmother checking her blood sugar with a small meter while a child leans on her shoulder.

terms.meaning: Passing from one person straight to another. A contagious disease is also called a catching disease.
terms.example: Measles is very contagious. Malaria is infectious but not contagious, because a mosquito must carry the germ.
terms.art: Two children sitting together, one coughing, with a dotted arrow from one to the other, and beside them a mosquito with an arrow between two other people.

terms.meaning: A change that an ill person feels or shows. Fever, cough, pain, rash and loose motions are symptoms.
terms.example: The symptoms of dengue are high fever, pain behind the eyes and aching joints.
terms.art: A child lying down with a thermometer, a hand on the forehead and small labels pointing to head, eyes and knees.

terms.meaning: The time between a germ getting into the body and the first symptom. The germ is multiplying during this time.
terms.example: Chickenpox has an incubation period of 10 to 21 days. Flu has 1 to 4 days.
terms.art: A calendar with one day circled and marked 'germ gets in' and a later day circled and marked 'first fever', with the days between shaded.

terms.meaning: A person who has a germ in their body and can pass the germ on, but has no symptoms.
terms.example: Some people carry the typhoid germ for years and feel well. Food they cook can still make others ill.
terms.art: A healthy-looking cook serving food, with a few small dots drawn on the hands and on the plate.

terms.meaning: An animal who carries a germ from one person to the next. Most vectors are insects or ticks.
terms.example: A female Anopheles mosquito is the vector of malaria. A female Aedes mosquito is the vector of dengue.
terms.art: Two mosquitoes side by side, one plain brown resting with her body tilted up and one with black and white striped legs.

terms.meaning: The drops that leave the mouth and nose in a cough, a sneeze or speech. Big droplets fall within about a metre. Very small ones, called aerosols, float in the air.
terms.example: The germs of flu, tuberculosis and measles ride in droplets and aerosols.
terms.art: A side view of a person coughing, with large drops curving down to the floor nearby and a fine mist drifting far across the room.

terms.meaning: The movement of fresh air through a room, which carries the old air out.
terms.example: Two open windows on opposite sides give good ventilation. The air comes in at one and goes out at the other.
terms.art: A room with windows open on two opposite walls and arrows showing air flowing in at one and out at the other.

terms.meaning: The state of a body that has lost too much water and salt. Loose motions and vomiting cause it.
terms.example: The signs are a dry mouth, sunken eyes, very little urine and great tiredness. ORS replaces the lost water and salt.
terms.art: A small child with dry lips being given sips from a steel tumbler by a parent, with a packet of ORS on the table.

terms.meaning: A time when many more people than usual in one place have the same disease.
terms.example: Cities in India often have a dengue epidemic after the monsoon. An epidemic that crosses many countries is a pandemic.
terms.art: A bar chart on a clinic wall with low bars for most months and three very tall bars after the rainy months.

terms.meaning: A non-infectious disease caused by too little of one nutrient in the food.
terms.example: Too little iron causes anaemia. Too little vitamin A causes night blindness. Too little iodine causes goitre.
terms.art: Three plates each with one food missing, labelled iron, vitamin A and iodine.

terms.meaning: A disease passed from parents to a child through their genes. Genes are the instructions inside every cell.
terms.example: Sickle cell disease and thalassaemia are inherited diseases of the blood. Nobody catches them.
terms.art: A simple family tree of parents and three children, with a round red blood cell and a curved sickle-shaped cell drawn beside it.

terms.meaning: A non-infectious disease made more likely by the way a person lives over many years. Genes and surroundings matter too.
terms.example: Type 2 diabetes and heart disease are more likely with tobacco, little movement and a lot of sugary, fried food.
terms.art: Two paths side by side: one with a person walking past a fruit stall, one with a person sitting with a cigarette and a fizzy drink.

terms.meaning: Anything that raises the chance of a disease. A risk factor does not decide who falls ill.
terms.example: Tobacco is a risk factor for cancer and for heart attack. Some smokers stay well, and some people who never smoked fall ill.
terms.art: Two groups of thirty small figures, one group with five figures coloured red and the other with fifteen coloured red.

terms.meaning: A substance made by the pancreas, an organ behind the stomach. Insulin lets sugar pass from the blood into the cells.
terms.example: In diabetes the body makes too little insulin or cannot use insulin well. So sugar stays in the blood.
terms.art: A blood vessel with small sugar cubes floating in it and a cell beside it whose door is being opened by a key labelled insulin.

terms.meaning: A tube that carries blood from the heart to the body. The heart muscle and the brain each have their own arteries.
terms.example: A heart attack happens when an artery of the heart is blocked. A stroke happens when an artery of the brain is blocked or bursts.
terms.art: A cut-away artery shown twice: one wide and clear, one narrowed by a yellow fatty layer with a dark clot blocking it.

terms.meaning: A disease in which some of the body's own cells keep dividing when they should stop. They form a lump or spread.
terms.example: Tobacco can cause cancer of the mouth, throat and lungs. Cancer is not catching.
terms.art: A row of neat, even cells, and beside them a crowded clump of uneven cells pushing the neat ones aside.

terms.meaning: A safe preparation that shows the body a harmless form or part of a germ. The body then gets ready for the real germ.
terms.example: Vaccines protect against measles, polio, tetanus, typhoid and some kinds of pneumonia.
terms.art: A health worker in a sari giving drops to a baby held by a parent, with a cold box on the table.

terms.meaning: The science of who falls ill, where and when. It studies many people together to find the cause.
terms.example: An epidemiologist marks cases on a map and on a calendar. The pattern often shows how the disease spreads.
terms.art: A woman at a desk marking dots on a town map, with a wall calendar behind her that has days ticked in red.

explanations.concept: Two kinds of disease: infectious and non-infectious
explanations.definition: An infectious disease is caused by a germ who gets into the body and multiplies. A non-infectious disease has no germ as its cause, and nobody catches it.
explanations.description: Germs are bacteria, viruses, fungi and tiny parasites who can live in a human body and harm it. When they get in and multiply, the person has an infection. Many infectious diseases pass on to other people, so one case can become many. A non-infectious disease begins inside the person's own body. The cause may be a missing nutrient, a gene from the parents, or slow damage over many years. It may also be something harmful in the air, water or food. These causes do not move from one person to the next. So the two kinds need different protection. For an infectious disease, we stop the germ from reaching the next person. For a non-infectious disease, we remove the cause or lower the risk. Doctors treat the two kinds differently too. Medicines that kill germs do nothing for diabetes or asthma.
examples: Infectious: common cold, flu, chickenpox, measles, cholera, typhoid, malaria, dengue, tuberculosis and HIV infection.
Non-infectious: diabetes, heart disease, stroke, most cancers, asthma, anaemia, goitre, sickle cell disease and cataract.
A broken arm and a snake bite are injuries. They are neither kind of disease.
explanations.art: A page divided in two, with germs drawn at the top of the left half and a body outline at the top of the right half, and disease names listed under each.

explanations.concept: Infectious does not always mean catching from a person
explanations.definition: Every contagious disease is infectious, but some infectious diseases never pass straight from one person to another. Their germs arrive by another road.
explanations.description: A contagious disease passes from person to person through the air, by touch, or through shared food and water. Colds, measles and chickenpox are contagious. Malaria is infectious, because a germ causes it. But a person with malaria is safe to sit beside. The germ must travel inside a mosquito. Tetanus is infectious too. The tetanus bacteria live in soil and enter through a deep cut. They do not pass from an ill person to a carer. Rabies reaches people through the bite of an infected dog or other animal. This difference matters in daily life. A person with malaria, tetanus or dengue does not need to be kept alone. The family needs mosquito nets or clean wounds instead. Keeping people away from someone who is not contagious helps nobody and hurts the ill person.
examples: Contagious: measles, chickenpox, flu, the common cold, tuberculosis of the lungs.
Infectious but not contagious: malaria, dengue, tetanus, rabies and Kyasanur Forest disease, which ticks carry in Karnataka.
A dog bite must be washed with soap and running water for 15 minutes. The person must see a doctor for the rabies vaccine the same day.
explanations.art: A child sitting on the bed of a parent who has malaria, both under a mosquito net, with a mosquito outside the net.

explanations.definition: Germs reach a new person by five main roads: the air, water and food, insects and ticks, touch, and blood and other body fluids.
explanations.description: In this unit we call each way a germ can travel a road. A road is simply the route from one body to the next. Each germ uses mostly one road, and the road decides the protection. Air: the germs leave in coughs, sneezes and speech, and the next person breathes them in. Water and food: the germs leave in the stools of an ill person and reach water, hands, flies or food. The next person swallows them. Insects and ticks: a mosquito or tick takes the germ in with blood and passes the germ on with her next bite. Touch: the germs pass by skin, or by things such as towels, combs and door handles. Blood and body fluids: the germs pass when the blood of an infected person enters another body. A doctor who knows the road can stop a disease without a medicine. Boiling water blocks the water road. A net blocks the mosquito road. An open window thins out the germs on the air road.
examples: Air: cold, flu, measles, chickenpox, tuberculosis, pneumonia, COVID-19.
Water and food: cholera, typhoid, diarrhoea, dysentery, hepatitis A, polio.
Insects and ticks: malaria, dengue, chikungunya, filariasis, Kyasanur Forest disease.
Touch: ringworm, scabies, sore eyes, head lice.
Blood and body fluids: HIV infection, hepatitis B.
explanations.art: Five small panels labelled air, water and food, insects, touch and blood, each with a simple picture: a cough, a glass of water, a mosquito, two hands and a syringe.

explanations.concept: Symptoms: what an illness shows, and what causes them
explanations.definition: A symptom is a change that an ill person feels or shows. Many symptoms of infection are made by the body's own defences.
explanations.description: A germ gets in and multiplies for some days before anything is felt. This time is the incubation period. Then symptoms begin. Fever is the body raising its own temperature, which slows many germs. A cough and a runny nose push germs out of the airways. Loose motions flush germs out of the gut. Swelling and redness show that blood and defender cells have arrived. Some symptoms help the germ too. A cough carries the germ to the next person, and loose motions carry the germ to water. Doctors read the set of symptoms to guess the disease, and then test to be sure. A fever with shivering every second day points to malaria, and a blood test confirms it. Non-infectious diseases have symptoms too, but they usually come slowly. Great thirst and much urine point to diabetes. Some people have a germ and no symptoms at all. They are carriers, and they can still pass the germ on.
examples: Measles: fever, cough, red eyes, then a red rash that starts on the face.
Typhoid: a fever that climbs over several days, with headache and stomach pain.
Diabetes: great thirst, much urine, tiredness and wounds that heal slowly.
explanations.art: A body outline with labels at the forehead (fever), nose (runny nose), chest (cough), belly (loose motions) and skin (rash).

explanations.concept: Diseases of dirty water and food
explanations.definition: Cholera, typhoid, diarrhoea, dysentery and hepatitis A spread when germs from the stools of an ill person reach water or food.
explanations.description: The germs leave the body in stools. They reach drinking water where sewage leaks or where people have no toilets. Unwashed hands and flies carry them to food. Cholera causes sudden, watery loose motions, many times a day. Diarrhoea means loose, watery stools from any cause. Dysentery is loose stools with blood or mucus. All three can dry the body out within hours, and this dehydration is the danger. Small children are at most risk. The treatment is oral rehydration solution, called ORS, given in sips again and again. A doctor is needed if the child cannot drink or passes blood. Typhoid causes a fever that climbs over days, with headache and stomach pain. It needs a doctor and an antibiotic. Hepatitis A harms the liver and turns the eyes and skin yellow, which is called jaundice. Protection is the same for all. Drink boiled or filtered water, wash hands with soap, cover food, and use a toilet. Vaccines protect against typhoid, hepatitis A and rotavirus. Rotavirus is the commonest cause of severe diarrhoea in babies. Gagandeep Kang, a doctor and scientist in Vellore, took a leading part in testing the first rotavirus vaccine made in India.
examples: Cholera: many watery stools, vomiting and fast dehydration.
Typhoid: a slowly rising fever for a week or more.
Hepatitis A: fever, no wish to eat, dark urine and yellow eyes.
explanations.art: A hand pump beside an open drain, a fly on uncovered food and a child washing hands with soap, joined by arrows that are crossed out at the soap.

explanations.definition: Malaria, dengue, chikungunya and filariasis are infectious diseases whose germs travel inside mosquitoes. They do not pass straight from person to person.
explanations.description: Only female mosquitoes bite, because they need blood to make eggs. When a female bites an infected person, she takes in the germ. The germ multiplies inside her for some days. Then she passes the germ on with her bites. Malaria is caused by a parasite called Plasmodium. The female Anopheles mosquito carries the parasite, and she bites mostly at night. The symptoms are fever with shivering and then sweating, often every second or third day. Dengue is caused by a virus. The Aedes mosquito carries the virus. She has striped legs, bites in the daytime, and lays eggs in clean standing water. Dengue brings high fever, pain behind the eyes, joint pain and sometimes a rash. Chikungunya brings fever and very painful joints. Filariasis is caused by thread-like worms, carried by Culex mosquitoes. After many years the legs can swell greatly. Any fever that lasts more than two days needs a blood test. Protection means sleeping under a net and covering arms and legs. It also means emptying standing water every week from coolers, pots and tyres. Mosquitoes need about a week to grow from egg to adult.
examples: Malaria: fever with shivering, then sweating, then a gap.
Dengue: sudden high fever with pain behind the eyes and in the joints.
Filariasis: no early symptoms, then swelling of a leg after years.
explanations.art: A flowerpot saucer of clear water with small wriggling larvae in it, and a striped-legged mosquito resting on the rim.

explanations.concept: Diseases that travel through the air
explanations.definition: Colds, flu, measles, chickenpox, tuberculosis and many kinds of pneumonia spread when a person breathes in germs that another person breathed out.
explanations.description: Coughing, sneezing, singing and talking send out drops of every size. Big droplets fall within about a metre. Very small ones, called aerosols, float for minutes or hours in a closed room. Colds and flu are caused by viruses. They bring a runny nose, sore throat, cough and, with flu, fever and body ache. Rest and warm drinks help, and antibiotics do not. Getting wet in the rain does not cause a cold, because a cold needs a virus. Pneumonia is an infection deep in the lungs. The signs are fast breathing, fever and chest pain, and the person needs a doctor at once. Tuberculosis, or TB, is caused by a slow-growing bacterium. The signs are a cough for more than two weeks, evening fever and loss of weight. TB is cured by taking medicines every day for at least six months. In India the tests and medicines are free at government health centres. Measles is one of the most contagious diseases known. Protection on the air road is fresh air, a mask on the ill person, a covered cough and vaccines. The BCG, measles and pneumonia vaccines are given to babies in India.
examples: Cold: runny nose, sneezing and sore throat for about a week.
TB: a cough for more than two weeks, with evening fever and weight loss.
Pneumonia: fast, hard breathing with fever.
explanations.art: A crowded closed room with a haze drawn in the air, beside the same room with two windows open and the haze thinning.

explanations.concept: HIV: how it spreads, and how it does not
explanations.definition: HIV is a virus who attacks the body's defender cells. HIV passes only through blood and a few other body fluids, never through everyday contact.
explanations.description: HIV stands for human immunodeficiency virus. Over years, the virus destroys defender cells in the blood. Without treatment, the body can no longer fight other infections. That late stage is called AIDS. HIV spreads in a few ways only. One is infected blood, for example on a shared needle or blade. Another is from a mother to her baby during pregnancy, at birth or through breast milk. The third is close physical contact between grown-ups. HIV does not spread by touching, hugging, shaking hands or sharing food. It does not spread by coughing, by toilets, or by mosquitoes. So a person with HIV can live, study, play and eat with everyone else. Medicines taken every day keep the virus very low, and the person can live a long life. In India these medicines are free at government centres. Medicines for the mother also protect her baby. There are two rules for children. Never touch a used needle or blade. Treat a person with HIV as kindly as anyone else.
examples: Safe: hugging, playing together, sharing a classroom, a meal or a toilet.
Not safe: sharing needles, blades or anything with blood on it.
A mosquito does not pass HIV on. The virus does not live or multiply inside mosquitoes.
explanations.art: Children playing a clapping game in a schoolyard and sharing a tiffin, with small green ticks beside each scene.

explanations.definition: Non-infectious diseases have causes inside the body or in the surroundings. The main groups are deficiency, inherited, long-term lifestyle, allergy, and harm from surroundings.
explanations.description: A deficiency disease comes from too little of one nutrient. Too little iron causes anaemia, with tiredness and pale skin. An inherited disease comes through the genes from both parents. Sickle cell disease bends some red blood cells into a curved shape, so they block small blood vessels. It is common in many Adivasi communities of central India. Long-term diseases build up over years. Heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes and many cancers belong here. In an allergy, the body's defences react strongly to something harmless, such as dust or pollen. In asthma the airways of the lungs narrow, and breathing becomes hard. An inhaler opens them. Some diseases come from the surroundings. Too much fluoride in well water damages teeth and bones in parts of Telangana and Rajasthan. Dirty air harms the lungs and the heart. Illnesses of the mind, such as depression, are non-infectious diseases too, and they can be treated. Non-infectious diseases now cause about six in every ten deaths in India.
examples: Deficiency: anaemia, night blindness, goitre, rickets.
Inherited: sickle cell disease, thalassaemia, haemophilia.
Long-term: heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, many cancers.
Allergy and surroundings: asthma, hay fever, fluorosis.
explanations.art: Five small panels labelled deficiency, inherited, long-term, allergy and surroundings, showing a pale child, a family tree, a heart, an inhaler and a village well.

explanations.concept: Heart attack and stroke: a blocked artery
explanations.definition: A heart attack happens when an artery that feeds the heart muscle is blocked. A stroke happens when an artery in the brain is blocked or bursts.
explanations.description: Arteries are tubes that carry blood from the heart. Over many years, a fatty layer can build up on the inside wall of an artery. The tube gets narrower. If a clot of blood forms on the fatty layer, the artery is blocked. The part beyond the block gets no oxygen, and its cells begin to die within minutes. In the heart, this is a heart attack. The signs are a heavy pain in the chest, pain in the arm or jaw, sweating and breathlessness. In the brain, this is a stroke. The signs come suddenly. One side of the face droops, one arm is weak, and speech is unclear. Both are emergencies, and every minute counts. In most Indian states the ambulance number is 108. The chance of both goes up with tobacco, high blood pressure, diabetes and little movement. Much salt and much fried food raise the chance too. It goes down with daily movement, plenty of vegetables and fruit, and no tobacco.
examples: Heart attack: chest pain that spreads to the arm or jaw, with sweating.
Stroke: a drooping face, a weak arm and unclear speech, all starting suddenly.
High blood pressure has no symptoms for years, so grown-ups need to have it measured.
explanations.art: A heart with its own small arteries drawn on the surface, one of them blocked by a dark clot, and the muscle beyond the block shaded grey.

explanations.concept: Diabetes: sugar that stays in the blood
explanations.definition: In diabetes, the level of sugar in the blood stays too high. The body makes too little insulin or cannot use insulin well.
explanations.description: Food is broken down into sugar, and the blood carries the sugar to every cell. Insulin is made by the pancreas. Insulin lets the sugar pass from the blood into the cells. In type 1 diabetes, the body's own defender cells destroy the cells that make insulin. It often begins in childhood. Sweets do not cause it, and the person needs insulin injections every day. In type 2 diabetes, the body still makes insulin, but the cells no longer respond well. It usually begins in adults and builds up slowly. It is more likely with extra weight, little movement, and when parents have diabetes. The symptoms of both are great thirst, much urine, tiredness, and wounds that heal slowly. High sugar over many years damages the eyes, kidneys, nerves and arteries. About 100 million people in India have diabetes. Type 2 can often be delayed or controlled by daily movement, less sugar and medicines. Old Indian doctors called the disease madhumeha, which means honey urine. They saw ants gather at the urine of people who had it.
examples: Type 1: begins suddenly, often in a child, and needs insulin for life.
Type 2: builds up over years, usually in adults.
A finger-prick blood test shows the sugar level in a few seconds.
explanations.art: A girl of about ten calmly giving herself an insulin injection in the upper arm before a meal, with her school bag beside her.

explanations.concept: Cancer: cells that do not stop dividing
explanations.definition: In cancer, some of the body's own cells keep dividing when they should stop. They form a lump called a tumour, or spread to other parts.
explanations.description: Every cell carries instructions called genes. Some genes tell the cell when to divide and when to stop. If these genes are damaged, the cell can go on dividing. Most damage is repaired, and most damaged cells die. Cancer begins when a damaged cell escapes both. Damage adds up over a lifetime, so cancer is more common in older people. Some things cause more damage. Tobacco is the biggest one. Smoking causes cancer of the lungs. Chewing tobacco and gutka cause cancer of the mouth, which is common in India. Too much strong sunlight, alcohol and some chemicals add to the damage. Cancer is not catching. But a few cancers are started by a germ who stays in the body for years. One virus, called HPV, starts cancer of the cervix, a part of the womb. A vaccine against that virus prevents most of those cancers. An Indian-made vaccine of this kind was approved in 2022. Many cancers can be cured when they are found early. Warning signs include a lump, a sore that does not heal, or bleeding with no cause.
examples: Mouth cancer: a white or red patch or a sore in the mouth that does not heal.
Lung cancer: most cases are in people who smoked for many years.
Some people get cancer with no known risk factor. Nobody is to blame for it.
explanations.art: A row of even cells with one cell dividing again and again into a crowded clump, and a cigarette and a gutka packet crossed out beside it.

explanations.concept: Risk: what raises the chance, and what it cannot tell
explanations.definition: A risk factor raises the chance that a person gets a disease. It does not decide what happens to any one person.
explanations.description: Infectious diseases have one necessary cause, which is the germ. Most non-infectious diseases have many causes that add up. Each one raises or lowers the chance. So two things are true together. People who use tobacco get lung cancer far more often than people who do not. Yet some smokers live long, and some people who never smoked get lung cancer. One person's story cannot settle the question. Only a comparison of large groups can. In 1950 the British scientists Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill compared hospital patients in London. Almost all the lung cancer patients had smoked, and heavy smokers were at most risk. Then they followed about 40,000 doctors for many years. The doctors who smoked died of lung cancer far more often. Some risk factors can be changed, such as tobacco, food, movement and dirty air. Others cannot, such as age and genes. Many depend on where a person lives and how much money the family has. So a risk is a reason to change what can be changed. It is never a reason to blame a person who is ill.
examples: Risk factors a person can change: tobacco, alcohol, little movement, much sugar and salt.
Risk factors a person cannot change: age, genes, the air of the city they live in.
In the Risk Dice Test, about half the people in the tobacco group stay well.
explanations.art: Two crowds of small figures, one labelled tobacco and one labelled no tobacco, with many more red figures in the first crowd but some in both.

explanations.concept: How people find out what kind of disease it is
explanations.definition: People find out how a disease spreads by studying many cases together: where they are, when they began, and what the ill people share.
explanations.description: This science is called epidemiology. A contagious disease leaves a pattern. Cases come in chains, and each new case had contact with an earlier one. The number of cases climbs faster and faster, and then falls. People who nurse the ill fall ill too. A disease that is not contagious leaves other patterns. The cases may be scattered. Or they may cluster around one shared thing, such as a well, a factory, a forest or a kind of food. A cluster alone does not prove that a disease is catching. A cluster shows only that the ill people share something. The next step is to find out what they share. Then comes a test. If the cause is removed, do the cases stop? Finding a germ in ill people is strong evidence. The German doctor Robert Koch set out rules for this in the 1880s. A germ must be found in the ill, grown alone, and shown to cause the disease.
examples: In the Two Maps Test, every new ill house on the catching map stands beside an earlier ill house.
People who drink from one well with too much fluoride all get stained teeth. That cluster is not catching.
Nurses who cared for pellagra patients never got pellagra. That was a clue that pellagra is not infectious.
explanations.art: Two town maps side by side, one with red dots spreading out from one house in rings and one with red dots gathered around a well.

explanations.concept: Prevention: block the road, or lower the risk
explanations.definition: An infectious disease is prevented by blocking the germ's road or by a vaccine. A non-infectious disease is prevented by removing its cause or lowering the risk.
explanations.description: Each protection works against some diseases and not others. Soap and clean hands block the touch road and part of the water and food road. Boiled or filtered water, covered food and toilets block the water and food road. Nets, covered skin and no standing water block the mosquito road. Fresh air, masks and covered coughs thin out the air road. Clean needles and tested blood block the blood road. A vaccine protects against one disease by any road. So a mask does nothing against malaria, and a mosquito net does nothing against cholera. For non-infectious diseases, the protection is different. Mixed food with iron, iodised salt and vegetables prevents deficiency diseases. An hour of movement each day, little sugar and salt, and no tobacco lower the risk of heart disease and diabetes. Clean air protects the lungs. Much protection cannot be done by one family alone. Clean piped water, sewers, vaccines, mosquito control and clean air are the work of a whole town. In India about a million women health workers called ASHAs carry vaccines, ORS and advice to homes. The World Health Organization honoured them in 2022.
examples: Cholera in a town stops when the water supply is made clean.
Iodised salt has made goitre rare in most of India.
A person with a cough who wears a mask protects everyone in the room.
explanations.art: Six shields in a row, each with a picture: soap, a pot of boiling water, a mosquito net, an open window, a vaccine vial and a pair of running shoes.

explanations.concept: Where the two kinds of disease meet
explanations.definition: The two groups are useful, but some diseases belong partly to both. A germ can start a disease that is not catching, and a non-infectious condition can open the way for a germ.
explanations.description: Most stomach ulcers were blamed on worry and spicy food. In the 1980s two Australian doctors showed that a bacterium causes most of them. A virus starts cancer of the cervix, and another virus starts much liver cancer. So vaccines against germs now prevent some cancers. The link runs the other way too. A child who gets too little food catches infections more easily and takes longer to recover. A person with diabetes is about three times as likely to fall ill with TB. One inherited condition even protects against an infection. People with one sickle cell gene are well, and they are less likely to die of malaria. The scientist Anthony Allison showed this in East Africa in 1954. This is why the sickle cell gene is common where malaria has been common. A body is one whole, so anything that changes one part can change how the body meets a germ.
examples: A bacterium, Helicobacter pylori, causes most stomach ulcers. Antibiotics cure them.
The hepatitis B vaccine, given to babies in India, prevents much liver cancer later in life.
Good food is part of the treatment of TB.
explanations.art: Two overlapping circles labelled infectious and non-infectious, with a stomach, a liver and a red blood cell drawn in the overlap.

explanations.concept: Is it possible to be too clean?
explanations.definition: Allergies and asthma have become much more common in the last hundred years. Some scientists think one cause is that children now meet fewer microbes early in life.
explanations.description: This idea is called the hygiene hypothesis. It does not say that washing hands is harmful. Hand washing, clean water and vaccines save millions of lives, and nobody disputes that. The debate is about which microbes a child's defences need to meet, and when.
examples: Children who grow up on farms with cows have less asthma than children in the nearby towns.
Hay fever was rare two hundred years ago and is common now.

perspectives.who: David Strachan, a British doctor, in 1989
perspectives.explanation: He studied thousands of British children. Those with more older brothers and sisters had less hay fever. He suggested that infections caught from older children in early life protect against allergy.

perspectives.who: Graham Rook, a British scientist, from the early 2000s
perspectives.explanation: He argued that colds and other infections are not what protects. What matters is meeting the harmless microbes of soil, farm animals and other people. Human bodies lived with these for millions of years. He calls them 'old friends'.

They say that allergy has several causes together, such as dirty air, changed food and genes. They warn that the phrase 'too clean' misleads people. Nobody should give up soap, clean water or vaccines because of it.

explanations.art: A child playing in garden soil beside a cow shed, and another child indoors with an inhaler, with a question mark between them.

agreed.text: Infectious diseases are caused by germs: particular bacteria, viruses, fungi or parasites.
agreed.evidence: In the 1870s and 1880s Robert Koch found the bacteria of anthrax, tuberculosis and cholera in ill humans and other animals. He grew each one alone and showed that it caused the disease. The same has since been done for hundreds of diseases.

agreed.text: Malaria is carried from person to person by female Anopheles mosquitoes, and not by air or touch.
agreed.evidence: In 1897 in Secunderabad, Ronald Ross found malaria parasites in the stomach wall of a mosquito who had fed on a patient. Where mosquitoes are controlled and people sleep under nets, malaria falls.

agreed.text: Tobacco causes lung cancer, mouth cancer and heart disease.
agreed.evidence: In 1950 Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill compared lung cancer patients with other patients in London hospitals. They then followed about 40,000 British doctors for decades. Smokers died of lung cancer many times more often, and those who stopped smoking lowered their risk.

agreed.text: Germs of tuberculosis and measles travel through the air in particles small enough to float for a long time.
agreed.evidence: In the 1950s Richard Riley and William Wells piped air from a tuberculosis ward in Baltimore to cages of guinea pigs. The guinea pigs caught tuberculosis from the air alone. When the air was treated with ultraviolet light first, they did not.

agreed.text: HIV does not pass on through touch, shared food, toilets, coughs or mosquito bites.
agreed.evidence: Studies of thousands of families living with a person who has HIV found no spread through everyday contact. The virus does not multiply inside mosquitoes.

agreed.text: In India, non-infectious diseases now cause more deaths than infectious diseases.
agreed.evidence: A large study of every Indian state counted the causes of death. In 1990, non-infectious diseases caused about 38 in every 100 deaths. In 2016 they caused more than 60 in every 100.

challenging.claim: Bad-smelling air from rubbish and marshes causes diseases such as cholera and malaria.
challenging.who: Most doctors in Europe and India until the late 1800s. The idea was called miasma.
challenging.for: Diseases were common in dirty, crowded and marshy places. Cleaning those places did reduce disease.
challenging.against: Germs were found for each disease, and their roads were traced to water and mosquitoes. A bad smell alone makes nobody ill. Yet the people who believed in miasma were right that fresh air matters. Germs of some diseases do float in the air of closed rooms.
challenging.context: This card is about an old explanation of what causes disease, called miasma.

challenging.claim: Getting wet in the rain or going out with wet hair gives you a cold.
challenging.who: A common belief in many countries
challenging.for: Colds are more common in the rainy and cold months. People often remember being wet before a cold began.
challenging.against: A cold is caused by a virus, and nobody catches a cold without meeting the virus. In wet and cold months people stay close together indoors with the windows shut, so viruses pass more easily. Some studies suggest a chilled nose fights viruses less well, but that is not settled.
challenging.context: This card is about whether rain and cold weather cause colds.

challenging.claim: A lifestyle disease is the ill person's own fault.
challenging.for: Tobacco, little movement and sugary food do raise the risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes and some cancers.
challenging.against: Risk also depends on genes, age, dirty air and the food a family can afford. Many people fall ill with no risk factor that they could have changed. A risk raises the chance for a group and does not explain one person's illness.
challenging.context: This card is about blame and the diseases linked to the way people live.

challenging.claim: Cancer never has anything to do with germs.
challenging.for: Cancer does not pass from one person to another, and it begins in the body's own cells.
challenging.against: The German scientist Harald zur Hausen found a virus, HPV, in cancers of the cervix in 1983 and 1984. A vaccine against that virus now prevents most of these cancers. The cancer itself is not catching, though the virus who starts it passes between people.
challenging.context: This card is about whether a germ can start a cancer.

challenging.claim: Becoming very overweight spreads from friend to friend, like an infection.
challenging.who: Nicholas Christakis and James Fowler, two American scientists, in 2007
challenging.for: They studied about 12,000 people over 32 years. When a person became very overweight, their close friends were more likely to become so too.
challenging.against: Other scientists used the same method on things that cannot spread, such as height and headaches. The method seemed to show that those spread too. Friends also choose each other because they are alike, and they share the same shops and streets.
challenging.context: This card is about whether habits and body weight can spread between people the way germs do.

challenging.claim: Flu and COVID-19 spread only by big droplets that fall within a metre or two.
challenging.for: People closest to an ill person are the most likely to catch these diseases.
challenging.against: In 2020, 239 scientists led by Lidia Morawska and Donald Milton wrote to the World Health Organization. They showed that people had been infected across large rooms with poor ventilation. Health agencies now agree that these viruses also float in small particles, so fresh air matters.
challenging.context: This card is about how far the germs in a cough can travel.

big_questions.q: One ill person looks the same whether their illness is catching or not. So how can anyone find out that an illness is catching? What do they have to look at?
big_questions.hint: Think about the Two Maps Test. What did you have to look at before you could tell the two maps apart?

big_questions.q: A cough pushes germs out of your lungs. The same cough carries the germ to the next person. Whose cough is it, yours or the germ's?
big_questions.hint: List who is helped by the cough. Is it possible that one action serves two living beings?

big_questions.q: A person with one sickle cell gene is protected from malaria. A person with two has a serious disease. Is that gene good or bad?
big_questions.hint: Think about where the person lives, and about how many copies of the gene they have.

big_questions.q: Clean water for a town prevents more illness than any medicine. Who should pay for it, and who should decide?
big_questions.hint: Think about who is protected when one family's water is clean, and who is protected when everyone's is.

big_questions.q: Tobacco raises the chance of cancer, but it does not decide it. Is it fair to blame an ill person for a disease that a risk made more likely?
big_questions.hint: Think about the Risk Dice Test. Could you tell which ill people in the tobacco group would have fallen ill anyway?

big_questions.q: People once drove away those who had leprosy or HIV, though neither spreads by everyday contact. Why does fear travel faster than facts?
big_questions.hint: Think about how people act before they know the road a germ travels.

big_questions.q: A germ who makes people very ill may stop them from meeting others. Is it better for a germ to be mild?
big_questions.hint: Compare a cold, which lets people walk about, with a disease that keeps people in bed.

story.title: The Tally on the Wall
story.note: Gowri, her family, Sharadakka and the tally are made up. These facts are real. In 1957, monkeys were found dead in the Kyasanur forest in Shimoga district, in what was then Mysore State and is now Karnataka. People in the villages nearby fell ill with a high fever. Scientists from the Virus Research Centre in Poona, now Pune, found a new virus in the dead monkeys and in the patients. They found that forest ticks carry the virus, and that the disease does not pass from one person to another. It is called Kyasanur Forest disease, or monkey fever. Most people recover, some die, and a vaccine now exists.
text: The langurs began to die in the month of March, when the forest floor above Gowri's village was deep in dry leaves.

Gowri's brother Shivu found the first one. He grazed the family's cattle under the trees, and he came home that evening very quiet. 'A big grey one,' he said. 'Lying on the leaves as if asleep. And another by the stream.'
Ajji, their grandmother, did not like it. 'When monkeys die, something is wrong in the forest,' she said.

Ten days later, the fever came to the village. Thimmappa the woodcutter had it first. His head hurt so badly that he could not open his eyes, and his whole body ached. Then two women from the far lane fell ill, and then the boy who herded goats.
People were afraid. 'It jumps from one person to the next,' they said. 'Do not go near those houses.' Nobody visited Thimmappa's wife any more. Nobody would lend her a pot.
Then Gowri's mother came back from gathering leaf litter in the forest, lay down, and did not get up. By night she was burning hot.
'Keep away from her,' the neighbours called from the gate. 'You will all get it.'

'Somebody must give her water,' said Gowri. She was eleven, and she was not going to leave her mother alone. So Gowri and Ajji nursed her. They wiped her face, fed her ragi gruel from a spoon and slept on the floor beside her mat.
Gowri waited to fall ill. She did not. Ajji did not. But Shivu, who had hardly gone near the sickroom, came home from the cattle one evening with the same fever.

That puzzled Gowri so much that she could not sleep. In the morning she took a piece of charcoal from the hearth and went to the back wall of the house. She drew a short line for every person in the village who had fallen ill. There were fourteen lines.

Beside each line she made a second mark if someone in that house had nursed the ill person. Then she walked from house to house and asked one question at each gate. 'Did the one who nursed fall ill too?'

Thimmappa's wife had nursed him for twelve days. She was well. The goat boy's mother was well. An old woman called Sharadakka had gone into four sick houses to help, because she said she was too old to be afraid. She was well.
'If it jumped from person to person,' Gowri said to Ajji, 'Sharadakka would have had it four times over.'
'Then where does it come from?' asked Ajji.
Gowri looked at her fourteen lines again. This time she asked a different question. What did these fourteen people do that the others did not?

Thimmappa cut wood. The two women gathered leaves. The goat boy took his goats under the trees. Her mother gathered leaves. Shivu grazed cattle. One man lived alone at the edge of the forest and met nobody for weeks, and he had the fever too.
Every one of the fourteen went into the forest. The weaver, the potter and the schoolmaster met ill people every day in the lanes. They never went into the forest, and not one of them was ill.
'It is in the forest,' said Gowri. 'It is where the langurs died.'

A week later a jeep came up the cart track with doctors from the laboratory in Poona. They went from house to house and took a little blood from each ill person. A young doctor stopped at the back wall and stared at the charcoal lines.
'Who made this?' he asked.
'I did,' said Gowri. She explained the lines and the second marks. She told him about Sharadakka, and about the man who lived alone. The doctor wrote for a long time in his notebook.
'We have been asking who met whom,' he said. 'You asked who went where. That is the better question.'

The doctors walked into the forest in tall boots. They found a dead langur and looked through the fur with a lens. They dragged a white cloth over the dry leaves and held the cloth up to the light. Small dark specks were walking on the cloth. They were ticks, each no bigger than a grain of ragi.

'The ticks drink the blood of the monkeys,' the young doctor told the village. 'Something in that blood makes monkeys and people ill. When a tick who carries it bites a person, the person gets the fever. An ill person cannot give it to you. A tick can.'

After that, things changed in the village. Shivu tied cloth round his ankles before he took the cattle out. The women rubbed oil on their legs and looked each other over for ticks when they came home. Nobody went near a dead monkey. They sent word to the forest guard instead.
And people went back into the sick houses. They carried gruel to Thimmappa's wife and lent her two pots.
Gowri's mother sat up on the ninth day and asked for buttermilk. Shivu was on his feet a week after her.
The rains washed most of the charcoal off the back wall that June. Gowri did not mind. She had already copied every line into the schoolmaster's old notebook, with the second marks beside them.
story.epiphany: The illness was caused by a germ, yet nobody caught it from an ill person. Gowri saw this in the pattern. The people who nursed the ill stayed well, and everyone who fell ill had been in the forest. Asking what the ill people shared showed the road the germ travelled.
ask: The people who nursed the ill stayed well. What does that tell you about how the fever spread?
Why did one ill person alone not show where the fever came from?
The villagers stayed away from the sick houses. Whom did that protect, and whom did it hurt?
Think of an illness in your own home. What would you ask to find out how it arrived?
art: A girl of eleven in a long skirt drawing short charcoal lines on the mud wall at the back of a tiled village house in the hills of Karnataka, with forest behind.

games.title: Which Road? A card game of how germs travel
games.context: This is a card game about diseases. Each card names a disease. You say whether a germ causes it, and which road the germ travels, or whether it has no germ at all.

printables.title: 24 disease cards to cut out (the road is on the back)

items.f: Common cold: runny nose and sneezing
items.b: AIR. Also TOUCH, from hands and tissues. Cover coughs, wash hands, open a window.

items.f: Measles: fever, red eyes, then a rash that starts on the face
items.b: AIR. One of the most contagious diseases. The measles vaccine protects babies.

items.f: Flu: fever, body ache and cough
items.b: AIR. A virus causes flu, so antibiotics do nothing. Rest, drinks and fresh air help.

items.f: Tuberculosis: a cough for more than two weeks, with evening fever
items.b: AIR. Free tests and medicines at government health centres. Every dose must be taken.

items.f: Cholera: many watery stools and vomiting
items.b: WATER AND FOOD. Boiled or filtered water, and ORS in sips to replace lost water.

items.f: Typhoid: a fever that climbs over a week
items.b: WATER AND FOOD. Safe water, covered food and washed hands. A vaccine exists.

items.f: Hepatitis A: yellow eyes and dark urine
items.b: WATER AND FOOD. Safe water and washed hands. A vaccine protects.

items.f: Rotavirus: severe watery loose motions in a baby
items.b: WATER AND FOOD. A vaccine protects babies. ORS replaces the lost water.

items.f: Malaria: fever with shivering every second or third day
items.b: INSECTS AND TICKS. A female Anopheles mosquito carries the germ and bites at night. A net blocks her.

items.f: Dengue: sudden high fever and pain behind the eyes
items.b: INSECTS AND TICKS. The Aedes mosquito bites by day and breeds in clean standing water.

items.f: Chikungunya: fever and very painful joints
items.b: INSECTS AND TICKS. Aedes mosquitoes carry the virus. Empty standing water every week.

items.f: Kyasanur Forest disease: fever after time in a forest
items.b: INSECTS AND TICKS. Ticks carry the virus. Cover legs and check the skin.

items.f: Filariasis: a leg that swells after many years
items.b: INSECTS AND TICKS. Culex mosquitoes carry thread-like worms. Nets and clean drains help.

items.f: Ringworm: a round, itchy patch on the skin
items.b: TOUCH. Use your own towel and comb. A fungus causes it, not a worm.

items.f: Scabies: itching at night between the fingers
items.b: TOUCH. Tiny mites pass by skin and shared bedding. The whole family is treated together.

items.f: Sore eyes: red, watery eyes in many children
items.b: TOUCH. Hands, towels and rubbed eyes carry the germ. Wash hands and use your own towel.

items.f: HIV infection: defender cells destroyed over many years
items.b: BLOOD AND BODY FLUIDS. Never by touch, food or mosquitoes. Never touch a used needle.

items.f: Hepatitis B: tiredness and yellow eyes, harm to the liver
items.b: BLOOD AND BODY FLUIDS. The hepatitis B vaccine, given to babies in India, protects.

items.f: Type 2 diabetes: great thirst, much urine, slow healing
items.b: NO GERM. Movement every day, less sugar and a healthy weight lower the risk.

items.f: Heart attack: heavy chest pain that spreads to the arm
items.b: NO GERM. A blocked artery. Movement, no tobacco, less salt and less fried food lower the risk.

items.f: Asthma: wheezing and tight breathing
items.b: NO GERM. The airways react to smoke, dust or pollen. Clean air and an inhaler help.

items.f: Anaemia: tiredness and pale skin
items.b: NO GERM. Too little iron in the food. Greens, dal and jaggery help.

items.f: Mouth cancer: a sore in the mouth that does not heal
items.b: NO GERM. Tobacco and gutka are the main cause. Nobody catches it.

items.f: Sickle cell disease: pain and tiredness from curved red blood cells
items.b: NO GERM. Inherited from both parents. Nobody catches it.

printables.title: A mat with six spaces
items: INSECTS AND TICKS: carried by a bite
BLOOD AND BODY FLUIDS: blood or other fluids of an infected person
NO GERM: not an infection, and nobody catches it

rules: Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, disease side up.
On your turn, read the top card aloud. Say if a germ causes the disease. Then say the road or NO GERM.
Turn the card over. A right space is worth 2 points.
If you said the right kind of disease but the wrong space, take 1 point.
Name one protection from the back of the card for 1 bonus point.
Put the card on its space on the mat. When the pile is finished, the player with the most points wins.
Playing alone: the most you can score is 72 points. Try for 54 or more, then play again and beat your score.

ask.q: Malaria is infectious, but a person with malaria is safe to sit beside. Which space shows why?
good: Insects and ticks. The germ needs a mosquito to carry her from one person to the next.

ask.q: Which card made you change your mind about how a disease spreads?
good: Any card, with a reason. For example scabies, which passes by touch, or hepatitis B, which passes by blood.

flow.parent: A good answer names the road and says what carries the germ. For no-germ cards, listen for 'it starts inside the body' or 'it comes from food, genes or smoke'. Hepatitis B and C are blood diseases. HIV is on the blood space as well.

check.q: Scabies and malaria are both infectious. Why are they on different spaces?
options: Scabies passes by touch, malaria by a mosquito bite
Malaria is much more serious than scabies
Scabies has no germ, so it sits elsewhere
check.why: The roads differ. Scabies mites pass by skin and shared bedding. A malaria parasite needs a mosquito to carry her. Picking the second option mixes up how serious a disease is with the road it uses.

games.title: Which Shield? A game of stopping illness before it starts
games.context: This is a card game about protection. Each card describes a real situation. You say which shield stops the illness, or lowers the risk of it.

printables.title: 20 situation cards to cut out (the best shield is on the back)

items.f: Many children in one lane have loose motions after drinking from an open stored pot.
items.b: CLEAN WATER AND FOOD. Boil or filter the water, cover the pot and wash hands.

items.f: Five children in one class have round, itchy patches on their skin.
items.b: SOAP AND CLEAN HANDS. Wash after any contact, and use only your own towel and comb.

items.f: A family sleeps near a pond, and two of them have fever with shivering.
items.b: NET, COVERED SKIN, NO STANDING WATER. A net over each bed blocks the Anopheles mosquito.

items.f: A clinic room has its only window shut, and a child inside is coughing.
items.b: FRESH AIR AND A COVERED COUGH. Open the window and the door on the other side.

items.f: A baby is nine months old and is due the measles shot.
items.b: VACCINE. Measles spreads very easily through the air, so the vaccine is the best shield.

items.f: A roadside barber uses one blade on every customer.
items.b: CLEAN NEEDLES AND BLADES. A new blade for each person, or a blade that is boiled or sterilised.

items.f: A grown-up whose parent has diabetes sits for most of the day.
items.b: CHANGE THE CAUSE. Movement every day, less sugar and a healthy weight lower the risk.

items.f: A teenager chews gutka every day.
items.b: CHANGE THE CAUSE. Stop tobacco. Mouth cancer begins with damage that adds up over the years.

items.f: Children in a hill village have swollen necks, called goitre.
items.b: CHANGE THE CAUSE. Iodised salt gives the iodine that is missing.

items.f: A fruit cart sells cut fruit uncovered, with flies on it.
items.b: CLEAN WATER AND FOOD. Cover the food and keep flies away. Wash hands before handling it.

items.f: A girl gets a deep cut from a rusty nail.
items.b: VACCINE. The tetanus vaccine, and washing the cut well. Tetanus bacteria live in soil.

items.f: After the rains, water stands in old tyres and coolers, and dengue cases rise.
items.b: NET, COVERED SKIN, NO STANDING WATER. Empty and scrub containers every week.

items.f: A grandfather is taking TB medicine and sits in a closed, crowded room.
items.b: FRESH AIR AND A COVERED COUGH. Open windows and cover coughs. The medicine soon lowers his chance of spreading TB.

items.f: A cook comes out of the toilet and goes straight into the kitchen.
items.b: SOAP AND CLEAN HANDS. Wash with soap for 20 seconds before touching food.

items.f: A girl of 11 is offered a vaccine against HPV.
items.b: VACCINE. HPV starts most cancers of the cervix, a part of the womb. The vaccine prevents them.

items.f: A child with asthma coughs in a kitchen full of smoke.
items.b: CHANGE THE CAUSE. Clean the air with a chimney, a cleaner fuel or an open window.

items.f: A grown-up's blood test shows low iron.
items.b: CHANGE THE CAUSE. Eat iron-rich food, such as greens, dal, jaggery and, for some, meat or eggs.

items.f: Children walk through a forest where ticks live.
items.b: NET, COVERED SKIN, NO STANDING WATER. Long sleeves, trousers tucked into socks, and a skin check at the end of the day.

items.f: After floods, sewage leaks into a town's well.
items.b: CLEAN WATER AND FOOD. Fix the pipes and clean the water. This is work for a whole town, not one family.

items.f: Sore eyes spread through a whole class, and the children share one towel.
items.b: SOAP AND CLEAN HANDS. Wash hands, do not rub the eyes and do not share towels.

items: NET, COVERED SKIN, NO STANDING WATER
FRESH AIR AND A COVERED COUGH

On your turn, read the top card aloud. Say which shield stops the illness, and say what the shield blocks.

If you did not name it, put the card on its shield on the mat.
