flow.context: This is the first step of Which Shield? Here you set up the situation cards and the mat of seven shields.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to read the top card. 2. Say the best shield and what it blocks. 3. Turn the card over to check.
flow.say: Take turns. Read the card aloud and give your answer. Then turn the card over. If you were wrong, say why the other shields would not help.
flow.kid: Read the card. Which shield fits? Say what it blocks. Then turn the card over.

ask.q: A mask does nothing against malaria. Why not?
good: Malaria travels by a mosquito bite, not through the air.
A mask blocks the air road, and malaria does not use it.

ask.q: Which cards could a single family not fix alone?
good: The town's well after the floods.
Anything that needs clean piped water, drains or vaccine supplies for everyone.

flow.parent: Many cards have a second true answer. Hands help with most diseases of the water and food road. Count it as the extra shield. Ask what the shield blocks if the answer is only a name.
flow.context: This is the main part of Which Shield? Here you read each situation and choose the shield that blocks the road or removes the cause.

flow.do: 1. Count your cards. 2. Look at the CHANGE THE CAUSE pile. 3. Ask why this shield has no germ to block.
flow.say: Look at the CHANGE THE CAUSE pile. What is different about these illnesses? Why can a vaccine or a net not help here?
flow.kid: Count your cards. Then look at the CHANGE THE CAUSE pile together.

check.q: A family boils all their water. Which illness does this shield not protect against?
options: Typhoid
Diabetes
Cholera
check.why: Boiling kills germs in water, so it protects against typhoid and cholera. Diabetes has no germ in the water behind it, so another shield is needed. Picking typhoid or cholera usually means forgetting that those two travel by water.

flow.context: This is the last step of Which Shield? Here you count your cards and think about which illnesses have no germ to block.

experiments.title: The Two Maps Test: can a map show whether an illness is catching?
experiments.context: In this experiment you use a die to make two maps of 36 houses. On one map an illness passes from house to house. On the other map the illness is not catching. You will find out whether a map alone can show that an illness is catching.
experiments.question: Two streets have the same number of ill houses. One illness is catching and the other is not. Is there anything on a map that shows which is which?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Both maps will end with the same number of ill houses. Which of these will be different on the two maps: where the ill houses are, how many fall ill each day, or nothing at all? On the map where the illness is not catching, will any ill houses stand side by side? Why do you think so? Write your guess and your reason.
experiments.fair_test: Both maps have 36 houses, the same die and the same number of ill houses at the end. Only the rule for falling ill changes. On map A a house can fall ill only from an ill neighbour. On map B the die picks houses anywhere.
results_table: New ill houses on each day
Ill houses beside an earlier ill house

materials.item: squared paper, or plain paper and a ruler
a die
a pencil and a red pencil or pen

schedule.what: Draw two maps of 36 houses. Fill map A by the catching rule and map B by the not-catching rule. Compare them three ways. Then try to tell two secret maps apart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for map A and map B. Make a bar chart of the new ill houses on each day, one chart for each map. Draw it, or stack coins, one stack for each day. Then say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Write one sentence for each.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results from one pair of maps
cols: New ill houses on each day
Ill houses beside an earlier ill house
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a filled table can look like. Your maps will be different, because the die decides.

setup.art: A sheet of squared paper with a 6 by 6 grid of houses, the rows and columns numbered 1 to 6, and a 1 written in the house at row 3, column 3.
setup.caption: 1. Draw 36 houses in 6 rows of 6. Number the rows and columns.

setup.art: The same grid with a 1 in one house and the number 2 in three houses that share a side with that house, and a die showing 3 beside the paper.
setup.caption: 2. Map A: roll for each well neighbour of a newly ill house. On 1, 2, 3 or 4, the neighbour falls ill.

setup.art: A second 6 by 6 grid with day numbers scattered across it in single houses, and a die beside the paper.
setup.caption: 3. Map B: two rolls pick a row and a column. That house falls ill.

setup.art: A child circling in red each numbered house that has a smaller number in a house beside it.
setup.caption: 4. On both maps, circle each ill house that stands beside an earlier ill house. Count the circles.

flow.do: 1. Draw two grids of 6 rows and 6 columns. 2. Number the rows 1 to 6 down the side and the columns 1 to 6 along the top. 3. Label one grid 'A: catching' and the other 'B: not catching'. 4. Read the question aloud and ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: Each square is one house. Both maps will end with the same number of ill houses. What do you think will be different about them? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Draw two grids of 36 houses. Number the rows and the columns. Label them A and B. Then tell your grown-up what you guess will be different, and why.
flow.parent: Many children guess that nothing on the map can show it, or that the catching map will simply have more ill houses. Write the guess down and do not correct it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Two Maps Test. Here you draw two maps of 36 houses and guess how a catching illness will look different from one that is not catching.

flow.do: 1. On map A, write 1 in the house at row 3, column 3. 2. For day 2, find each well house that shares a side with the house marked 1. 3. Roll once for each. On 1, 2, 3 or 4, write 2 in that house. 4. For day 3, do the same around every house marked 2. 5. Go on, one day at a time. Finish the day on which the map reaches 12 ill houses, then stop.
flow.say: On this map the illness passes only to a house next door. A house passes the illness on for one day. Then the people there are getting better.
flow.kid: Write 1 in row 3, column 3. Roll for each well house beside it. On 1 to 4, that house falls ill. Write the day number. Stop when 12 houses or more are ill.

ask.q: Why does a house marked 1 not pass the illness on again on day 3?
good: In this model a house passes the illness on for one day only.
The people there are getting better.

flow.parent: Houses that touch only at a corner are not neighbours. If two ill houses share a well neighbour, roll once for each of them. About once in 30 maps the illness stops before 12 houses. Real outbreaks sometimes stop this way too. If that happens, start map A again.
flow.context: In this step of the Two Maps Test you fill map A. On map A an illness passes from an ill house to the houses beside it, by the roll of a die.

flow.do: 1. Count the ill houses on map A. Map B must reach the same number. 2. On map B, roll twice: the first roll is the row, the second is the column. Write 1 in that house. 3. Roll twice again for a second house on day 1. 4. On each new day, pick two houses in the same way and write the day number. 5. If the die picks a house that is already ill, nothing happens. 6. Stop as soon as map B has as many ill houses as map A.
flow.say: On this map nobody catches anything. Each day the die picks two houses anywhere in the town. Their neighbours make no difference at all.
flow.kid: Count the ill houses on map A. On map B, roll for a row and a column. That house falls ill. Pick two houses each day. Stop at the same number as map A.
flow.parent: Map B usually takes 7 to 10 days. That is about twice as long as map A.
flow.context: In this step of the Two Maps Test you fill map B. On map B the illness is not catching, so the die picks ill houses anywhere in the town.

flow.do: 1. Put the maps side by side. Ask what your child notices first. 2. On each map, circle in red every ill house that has a smaller number in a house beside it. 3. Count the circles on each map. 4. For each map, list how many houses fell ill on day 1, day 2, day 3 and so on. 5. Fill in the table.
flow.say: Both maps have the same number of ill houses. Look at where they are. Now look at the day numbers. What do you notice?
flow.kid: Look at both maps. What is different? Circle each ill house beside an earlier ill house. Count the circles. Then count the new ill houses for each day.

ask.q: On map A, how many ill houses stand beside an earlier ill house?
good: All of them except the first house.

ask.q: Map B has some ill houses side by side too. How did that happen?
good: By chance. The die happened to pick houses that are neighbours.

ask.q: How do the numbers of new ill houses change from day to day on each map?
good: On map A they grow each day.
On map B they stay at about two a day.

flow.parent: On map A every ill house but the first is circled. On map B usually between 3 and 9 are circled, by chance alone. So one pair of ill neighbours proves nothing. The whole pattern is the evidence.
flow.context: In this step of the Two Maps Test you compare map A, where the illness was catching, with map B, where it was not. You look at where the ill houses are and on which day each fell ill.

flow.do: 1. Send your child out of the room. 2. Make two new maps, one by each rule, with the same number of ill houses. Do not label them. 3. Call your child back and hand over both maps. 4. Ask which map shows the catching illness, and what the evidence is.
flow.say: One of these maps was made by the catching rule and one by the other rule. Which is which? Show me the evidence on the map.
flow.kid: Someone makes two secret maps for you. Find the catching one. Use the circles and the day numbers. Say your evidence. Working alone? Make a new pair of maps and check your first result.

check.q: A map has 14 ill houses. Only 5 stand beside an earlier ill house. About 2 fell ill each day. Which rule made this map?
options: The catching rule
The not-catching rule
Nobody can tell from a map
check.why: Under the catching rule every ill house but the first stands beside an earlier one, and the daily numbers grow. Here most ill houses have no earlier ill neighbour and the daily number is steady. Picking 'the catching rule' usually means counting any ill neighbours as proof. Some houses are neighbours by chance.

flow.parent: This takes you about 8 minutes. To save time, your child can make the second pair while you make the first. A child working alone repeats steps 2 to 4 and sees whether the result holds.
flow.context: In this step of the Two Maps Test you are given two unlabelled maps of ill houses. You work out which was made by the catching rule and which by the not-catching rule.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to point at any one ill house on map B. 2. Ask whether that one house alone shows which map it is on. 3. Ask for the three sentences: what I thought, what I saw, why it happened.
flow.say: Point at one ill house. Looking at that house alone, could you tell which map this is? So what did you have to look at?
flow.kid: Point at one ill house on map B. Then say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

ask.q: What did you have to look at to tell the maps apart?
good: Many houses together.
Where the ill houses were and when each one fell ill.

flow.parent: A strong answer says that one ill house looks the same on both maps. The difference is in how the ill houses are joined in place and in time. This is how real diseases are sorted into catching and not catching.
flow.think: A doctor sees one ill person at a time. Who would be able to see the whole map?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Two Maps Test. Here you say what the two maps showed about telling a catching illness from one that is not catching.

experiments.title: The Risk Dice Test: does a risk decide who falls ill?
experiments.context: In this experiment a die stands for chance in two groups of 30 people. One group uses tobacco and one does not. A risk is something that makes an illness more likely. You will find out what a risk does to a group, and what it can tell you about one person.
experiments.question: Tobacco raises the chance of serious illness. Does that mean every tobacco user falls ill, and nobody else does? What can a risk tell us about one person?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Each group has 30 people. In the group without tobacco, a roll of 1 means illness. In the tobacco group, a roll of 1, 2 or 3 means illness. How many people will fall ill in each group? Will anyone without tobacco fall ill? Will anyone with tobacco stay well? Why do you think so? Write your guesses and your reasons.
experiments.fair_test: Both groups have 30 people and use the same die, with one roll for each person. Only the numbers that mean illness change. The chances are made up to suit a die. Real chances differ from disease to disease.

materials.item: paper and a pencil
a red pencil or pen
a die

schedule.what: Draw two groups of 30 people. Roll once for each person and colour the ill ones. Compare the groups. Then repeat with small groups of 6.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for the two groups of 30. Then make a second table for six rounds with groups of 6. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Write one sentence for each.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: people who fell ill out of 30
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a chart can look like. Your numbers will be different, because the die decides.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with two blocks of 30 small circles each, in 5 rows of 6, one block labelled No tobacco and one labelled Tobacco.
setup.caption: 1. Draw two groups of 30 circles. Each circle is one person.

setup.art: A child rolling a die beside the first block of circles, with a few circles coloured red.
setup.caption: 2. Roll once for each person. Colour the person red if the roll means illness.

setup.art: The two blocks side by side, the first with about five red circles and the second with about fifteen.
setup.caption: 3. Count the red circles in each group and compare.

flow.do: 1. Draw two blocks of 30 circles, in 5 rows of 6. 2. Label one 'No tobacco' and the other 'Tobacco'. 3. Explain the two rules. 4. Ask for the guesses and reasons, and write them down.
flow.say: Each circle is one person, followed for many years. Without tobacco, only a 1 means illness. With tobacco, a 1, 2 or 3 means illness. What will happen in each group? Why?
flow.kid: Draw two groups of 30 circles. Label them No tobacco and Tobacco. Guess how many fall ill in each group. Will anyone without tobacco fall ill? Tell your grown-up why.
flow.parent: Many children expect nobody in the first group to fall ill and nearly everyone in the second. Write the guess down.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Risk Dice Test. Here you draw two groups of 30 people and guess how many in each group will fall ill.

flow.do: 1. Start with the 'No tobacco' group. Roll once for each circle. 2. If the roll is 1, colour that circle red. 3. Then do the 'Tobacco' group. Colour a circle red on a roll of 1, 2 or 3. 4. Count the red circles in each group and fill in the table.
flow.say: Roll once for each person. The die stands for everything we cannot see: luck, the body that person was born with, and the rest of their life.
flow.kid: Roll once for each person. In the first group, colour a 1 red. In the tobacco group, colour 1, 2 and 3 red. Count the red circles.
flow.parent: Expect about 5 red circles in the first group, and anything from 2 to 9 is common. Expect about 15 in the tobacco group, and 10 to 20 is common.
flow.context: In this step of the Risk Dice Test you roll a die once for each of 60 people. The roll decides who falls ill in the group with tobacco and the group without.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to compare the two groups. 2. Point to one red circle in the 'No tobacco' group and ask how that happened. 3. Point to one uncoloured circle in the 'Tobacco' group and ask the same. 4. Point to one red circle in the 'Tobacco' group. Ask whether tobacco made this person ill.
flow.say: Look at this ill person in the tobacco group. Did the tobacco make them ill? Or would they have fallen ill anyway? How could we know?
flow.kid: Compare the groups. Find an ill person without tobacco. Find a well person with tobacco. Then point at one ill tobacco user. Why did that person fall ill?

ask.q: Did everyone in the tobacco group fall ill?
good: No. About half stayed well.

ask.q: For one ill person in the tobacco group, can you tell whether tobacco was the cause?
good: No. A roll of 1 would have made them ill in either group.
Only a 2 or 3 was because of the tobacco, and a real person does not show a number.

flow.parent: This is the heart of the test. The die shows what real life hides. Of about 15 ill people in the tobacco group, about 5 would have been ill without tobacco. Nobody can say which 5.

check.q: A man smoked all his life and stayed well until he was 90. What does this show?
options: Tobacco is harmless
A risk raises the chance but does not decide
He must have had special lungs
check.why: In the tobacco group about half the people stayed well, and the tobacco still tripled the number who fell ill. One person's story cannot show what a risk does. Picking 'tobacco is harmless' usually means judging from one case and not from the whole group.

flow.context: In this step of the Risk Dice Test you compare a group of 30 people with tobacco and 30 without. You ask what the result can tell you about any one person.

flow.do: 1. Now use small groups. Draw 6 circles for 'No tobacco' and 6 for 'Tobacco'. 2. Roll for all 12 people by the same rules. 3. Write how many fell ill in each small group. 4. Do this six times. 5. Count the rounds in which the 'No tobacco' group had as many ill people as the 'Tobacco' group, or more.
flow.say: A scientist with little money studies only 6 people in each group. Will the tobacco group always come out worse? Let's test that six times.
flow.kid: Now test small groups of 6 people. Roll for 6 without tobacco and 6 with. Write the two numbers. Do six rounds. Did tobacco always come out worse?

ask.q: In how many of the six rounds did the tobacco group not come out worse?
good: Often one round, sometimes none or two.

ask.q: Why are 30 people better than 6 for this test?
good: With few people, chance can hide the real difference.
Big groups even out the luck.

flow.parent: With groups of 6, the 'No tobacco' group has as many ill people or more in about one round in six. With groups of 30, that almost never happens. This is why health studies need thousands of people.
flow.context: In this step of the Risk Dice Test you repeat the test with small groups of 6 people. You find out whether a small study always shows the effect of a risk.

flow.do: 1. Look back at the guesses from the first step. 2. Ask for the three sentences: what I thought, what I saw, why it happened. 3. Ask what a risk factor is, in your child's own words.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Then tell me what a risk does, and what it does not do.
flow.kid: Read your first guess again. Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened. Then say what a risk does.
flow.parent: A strong answer says that a risk changes how many people in a group fall ill. It does not say who. So nobody should be blamed for an illness, and nobody should feel safe because one smoker stayed well.
flow.think: If you could not see the dice, how would you find out that tobacco was a risk at all?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Risk Dice Test. Here you say what the dice showed about what a risk does to a group and to one person.

experiments.title: One Opening or Two: which bottle clears smoke fastest?
experiments.context: In this experiment a plastic bottle stands for a room, and agarbatti smoke stands for the fine particles that float in a closed room. You test whether the smoke leaves faster through one opening or through two.
experiments.question: Fine particles from coughs can float in a closed room for a long time. Is one open window enough to clear them, or does a room need two openings?
experiments.predict: Guess first. A bottle full of smoke is tested three ways: closed, open at the top only, and open at the top and at a side window. Which will clear fastest? Will the bottle with one opening clear much faster than the closed bottle? Why do you think so? Write your guess and your reason.
experiments.fair_test: Use the same bottle, the same 30 seconds of smoke and the same spot on the table each time. Keep the fan at the same slow speed and the torch in the same place. Only the openings change.
results_table: Time until the haze was gone

materials.item: a clear 1-litre plastic bottle with its cap, washed and dry
an agarbatti in a stand, and a matchbox
a torch or a phone torch
a dark cloth or a dark book cover to stand behind the bottle
scissors or a knife, for a grown-up, and sticky tape
a clock or phone that shows seconds
a ceiling fan at its slowest speed, or a table near an open window

experiments.safety: A grown-up lights the agarbatti, holds the bottle over the smoke and does the cutting. Keep the glowing tip at least 5 centimetres from the plastic. Work near an open window and do not breathe the smoke on purpose. Anyone with asthma watches from across the room. Dip the agarbatti in water at the end.

schedule.what: Guess. Fill the bottle with smoke three times and test it closed, with one opening and with two openings. Time how long the haze lasts each time.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for the three trials. Write 'thick', 'thin' or 'gone' for the haze at each minute. Then say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Write one sentence for each.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
cols: Time until the haze was gone
example_chart.note: These results are made up, to show what a filled table can look like. Your times will depend on your bottle and on how much the air in the room moves.

setup.art: A grown-up holding a clear plastic bottle upside down above a smoking agarbatti in a stand, with grey smoke rising into the bottle.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up holds the bottle upside down over the smoke for 30 seconds, then caps it.

setup.art: The capped smoky bottle standing upright on a table in front of a dark cloth, with a torch beam shining through it from the side and showing a grey haze.
setup.caption: 2. Stand the bottle in front of a dark cloth. Shine a torch through the side.

setup.art: The same bottle with its cap off and a square window cut low in its side, the haze streaming out, and a clock beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Test it closed, then with the top open, then with the top and a side window open. Time the haze.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the bottle, the cap and where the side window will be cut. 2. Explain that the bottle stands for a room and the smoke for fine particles in the air. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write both down.
flow.say: This bottle is a small room. We will test it closed, with one opening and with two. Which will clear fastest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: The bottle is a small room. The smoke stands for fine particles in the air. Tell your grown-up your guess and why.
flow.parent: Many children expect one opening to work nearly as well as two. Write the guess down.
flow.context: This is the first step of One Opening or Two. Here you guess whether a bottle of smoke clears faster through one opening or through two.

flow.do: 1. Stand the lit agarbatti in its holder near an open window. 2. Hold the bottle upside down with its mouth 5 centimetres above the tip. Count 30 seconds. 3. Screw the cap on while the bottle is still upside down. 4. Stand the bottle on the table under the slow fan, in front of the dark cloth. 5. Shine the torch through the side. 6. Leave the cap on. At 1, 2 and 3 minutes, write whether the haze is thick, thin or gone.
flow.say: This is trial A, the closed room. Watch the grey haze in the torch beam. Is it getting thinner? Where could the smoke go?
flow.kid: A grown-up fills the bottle with smoke and caps it. Shine the torch through the side. Look at the haze each minute. Write thick, thin or gone.

ask.q: The bottle is closed. Why might the haze still get a little thinner?
good: Some smoke sticks to the inside of the bottle.
Some particles settle.

flow.parent: The haze shows best from the side, with the room light dim. In the closed bottle it should still be easy to see after 3 minutes. If you see no haze at the start, hold the bottle over the smoke for a full minute.
flow.context: This is trial A of One Opening or Two. Here a grown-up fills a bottle with agarbatti smoke and you watch how long the haze stays in the closed bottle.

flow.do: 1. Fill the bottle with smoke for 30 seconds again and cap it. 2. Stand it in the same spot. 3. Take the cap off and start the clock. 4. Write the haze at 1, 2 and 3 minutes. 5. Write the time when no haze shows in the torch beam. Stop at 5 minutes.
flow.say: This is trial B, a room with one open window. The smoke can leave only through the top. Watch the beam and tell me when the haze has gone.
flow.kid: Fill the bottle again. Put it in the same spot. Take the cap off and start the clock. Write the haze each minute. Stop when it is gone.
flow.parent: With one opening, the air inside has no easy way to be replaced. So the haze usually thins slowly. It may still be there at 5 minutes.
flow.context: This is trial B of One Opening or Two. Here the bottle of smoke has one opening at the top, and you time how long the haze lasts.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts a window about 4 centimetres square, low in the side of the bottle. 2. Cover the window with tape. 3. Fill the bottle with smoke for 30 seconds and cap it. 4. Stand it in the same spot, with the window facing the moving air. 5. Take off the cap and the tape together and start the clock. 6. Write the time when the haze has gone.
flow.say: This is trial C, a room with two openings. Air can come in at one and go out at the other. Watch closely, because this may be quick.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts a side window and tapes it shut. Fill the bottle again. Take off the cap and the tape together. Time the haze.

ask.q: What can the air do now that it could not do with one opening?
good: It can flow through: in at one opening and out at the other.
Fresh air can push the smoky air out.

flow.parent: With two openings the haze usually clears in well under a minute. If it does not, turn the window towards the fan or the open room window.
flow.context: This is trial C of One Opening or Two. Here the bottle of smoke has two openings, at the top and low in the side, and you time how long the haze lasts.

flow.do: 1. Dip the agarbatti in water. 2. Compare the three times in the table. 3. Ask for the three sentences: what I thought, what I saw, why it happened. 4. Walk through your home and find a room with two openings and a room with one.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Now, which room in our home is like bottle B? Which is like bottle C?
flow.kid: Compare the three times. Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened. Find a room at home with two openings.

check.q: A person with a cough rests in a room. Which gives the people who visit the best protection?
options: Door and window both shut
One window open
A window and the door on the far side open
check.why: With two openings on different sides, air flows through the room and carries floating particles out, as in bottle C. One opening lets air out only slowly, as in bottle B. Picking 'both shut' usually means thinking that outside air brings the illness in.

flow.parent: A strong answer says that smoke leaves when fresh air can flow through and push it out. Smoke is not germs. But the fine particles from a cough float and move in the same way.
flow.think: Smoke itself harms the lungs. Which non-infectious diseases does smoky air make more likely?
flow.context: This is the last step of One Opening or Two. Here you compare how fast smoke left a closed bottle, a bottle with one opening and a bottle with two openings.

activities.title: Our Family's Illness List: which illnesses were catching?
activities.context: In this activity you list the illnesses your family has had. For each one, you decide whether a germ was behind it, and how it probably travelled.

materials.item: a notebook page and a pencil
two or more grown-ups to ask

schedule.what: List eight illnesses your family has had. Decide for each one if it was catching, and which road or cause fits.

activities.record: Draw a table with four columns: the illness, did someone else at home get it too, the road or cause, and catching or not. Under the table, write one sentence about which road came up most.

setup.art: A child with a notebook sitting beside a grandmother, asking her a question, with a cup of tea between them.
setup.caption: 1. Ask a grown-up which illnesses the family has had. Write eight.

setup.art: A notebook page with a four-column table half filled in: cold, yes, air, catching.
setup.caption: 2. For each illness, fill in the columns.

setup.art: A child pointing at the last column of the table, with a pencil in the other hand.
setup.caption: 3. Count the catching ones. Look for the road that came up most.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to ask two grown-ups which illnesses the family has had. 2. They write eight, such as colds, fevers, loose motions, chickenpox, asthma or blood pressure. 3. Skip anything a person would rather not share.
flow.say: Which illnesses have we had in our family? Ask whoever you like. Write down eight. Nobody has to share anything private.
flow.kid: Ask two grown-ups which illnesses the family has had. Write eight. Skip anything private.
flow.parent: Good finds are colds, fever, loose motions, chickenpox, mumps, dengue, headaches, asthma, high blood pressure and sugar. Ordinary illnesses count. Write no names.
flow.context: This is the first step of Our Family's Illness List. Here you ask the family which illnesses they have had and write eight of them.

flow.do: 1. For each illness, ask whether another person at home fell ill soon after. 2. Decide which road fits: air, water and food, insects, touch or blood. 3. Write NO GERM if no germ causes it. 4. Write catching or not.
flow.say: Did someone else at home fall ill soon after? Which road did the germ probably use? Or is there no germ behind it?
flow.kid: For each illness, did someone else at home fall ill too? Name the road the germ used: air, water and food, insects, touch or blood. Or write no germ.

ask.q: Does one family's list prove that an illness is catching?
good: No. A few cases at home could be chance.
We would need many families, as in the Two Maps Test.

flow.parent: If you are unsure, say so and write a question mark. A doctor or the earlier cards will settle it. Colds are air. Loose motions are usually water and food. Asthma and blood pressure have no germ.
flow.context: In this step of Our Family's Illness List you decide, for each illness, which road or cause fits, and whether the illness was catching.

flow.do: 1. Count the catching illnesses and the not-catching ones. 2. Find the road that came up most. 3. Ask which protection would have blocked it.
flow.say: How many were catching? How many were not? Which road came up most? What would have blocked it?
flow.kid: Count the catching illnesses. Count the others. Which road came up most?

check.q: Most of a family's illnesses are colds and coughs. Which road do these mostly use?
options: Air
Water and food
Insects and ticks
check.why: Colds and coughs are caused by viruses that travel in the breath of other people. Picking water and food usually means thinking of any stomach upset. Colds can also pass by touch, but the air is the main road.

flow.context: This is the last step of Our Family's Illness List. Here you count the catching illnesses and find the road that came up most.

activities.title: Incubation Detective: when did the germ get in?
activities.context: In this activity you read made-up dates for three groups of people who each met an ill visitor. You work out which illness is which from the days between the visit and the first symptom.

materials.item: squared paper or a notebook page
a pencil and a ruler

schedule.what: Draw a line of days from 0 to 30. Mark the first-symptom days for three groups. Decide which illness each group had.

activities.record: Show your day line with three rows of dots, one row for each group. Draw it, or take a photo. Beside it, write the illness you think each group had, and one sentence of reasons.

setup.art: A line of days from 0 to 30 drawn across a page, with a small house at day 0 and a short mark for each day.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a line of days from 0 to 30. Day 0 is the day of the visit.

setup.art: The same line with three rows of coloured dots: the first row near days 2 to 4, the second row near days 9 to 21, the third near days 11 to 17.
setup.caption: 2. Mark each person's first-symptom day as a dot.

setup.art: A child holding a pencil between two dots and counting the days between them aloud.
setup.caption: 3. Compare the three rows. Which illness is which?

flow.do: 1. Draw a line of days from 0 to 30. 2. Read the table: flu 1 to 4 days, typhoid 6 to 30 days, chickenpox 10 to 21 days. 3. Explain that each visitor came on day 0 and was ill.
flow.say: Each group met one ill visitor on day 0. The days between the visit and the first symptom are the incubation period. Each illness has its own usual range.
flow.kid: Draw a day line from 0 to 30. Read the three ranges. Day 0 is the visit.
flow.parent: Typhoid most often shows up after one to two weeks, so the range is wide. Chickenpox is passed on from about one or two days before the rash. Many people can pass on a germ before they feel ill.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Incubation Detective. Here you draw a line of days and read the usual incubation periods of flu, typhoid and chickenpox.

flow.do: 1. Group P has first symptoms on days 2, 2, 3 and 4. 2. Group Q has them on days 7, 9, 12 and 21. 3. Group R has them on days 11, 13, 14 and 17. 4. Mark each one on the line with a dot or a bean, one row for each group.
flow.say: Here are the days when each person in each group first felt ill. Put a dot on the line for each. Then tell me what you notice.
flow.kid: Mark each first-symptom day with a dot or a bean. Use one row for each group. What do you notice?

ask.q: Which group can you name from the days alone?
good: Group P. Only flu shows its first symptoms in 1 to 4 days.

ask.q: Groups Q and R overlap. What else would you ask to tell them apart?
good: The symptoms: a slowly rising fever with stomach pain, or itchy blisters.
Where the people ate, and whether they had a rash.

flow.parent: Group P is flu. Group Q is typhoid, and group R is chickenpox. The ranges overlap, so the days alone cannot name Q and R. A doctor uses days and symptoms together.
flow.context: In this step of the Incubation Detective you mark first-symptom days for three groups and work out which group had flu.

flow.do: 1. Ask how long a visitor with flu leaves children at risk. 2. Ask the same for chickenpox. 3. Ask why a person well on day 5 may still be at risk after a chickenpox visit.
flow.say: A child is well on day 5 after a visitor with flu. Is that child probably safe from that visit? What about after a visitor with chickenpox? Why is it different?
flow.kid: Look at the flu range and the chickenpox range. Where does day 5 fall in each?

check.q: A child is well 22 days after meeting a visitor who had chickenpox. What is most likely?
options: The child did not catch it from that visit
The germ is still hiding and will show later
The child is a carrier
check.why: Chickenpox shows its first symptoms 10 to 21 days after the germ gets in. Day 22 is past the usual range, so the child most likely escaped. Picking the second option forgets that the incubation period has an end.

flow.parent: Flu is over its incubation period in about 4 days, so day 5 is nearly safe. Chickenpox needs up to 21 days. This is why a child exposed to a disease may be kept at home for a set number of days.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Incubation Detective. Here you use the incubation periods to say how long people must wait after meeting someone ill.

activities.title: Our Emergency Card: who to call and what to say
activities.context: In this activity you make a card for your home with the emergency numbers and the warning signs of a heart attack, a stroke and dehydration. Then you practise a call.

materials.item: a card or a sheet of paper cut to the size of a postcard
a pen and a pencil
a phone or a pretend phone

schedule.what: Write the numbers and the warning signs on a card. Practise a call with a grown-up playing the operator.

activities.record: Make the card. It has the emergency numbers, the address in words, the warning signs for a heart attack and a stroke, and the signs of dehydration. Stick it near the phone or on the fridge.

setup.art: A postcard-sized card on a table with the numbers 108 and 112 written large at the top and an address line below.
setup.caption: 1. Write the numbers and your address on a card.

setup.art: A card with three small boxes headed Heart attack, Stroke and Dehydration, each with signs written in.
setup.caption: 2. Add the warning signs for three emergencies.

setup.art: A child holding a pretend phone while a parent in a chair plays the operator.
setup.caption: 3. Practise the call. Say who, where and what.

flow.do: 1. Write 108 for an ambulance and 112 for any emergency. 2. Write the address in words, with a landmark. 3. Add the name and number of a neighbour and the nearest hospital. 4. Check which numbers work in your state.
flow.say: Which number do we call for an ambulance? Write it large. Now write our address in words, with a landmark that a stranger could find.
flow.kid: Write 108 and 112 large. Write our address and a landmark. Add the nearest hospital.
flow.parent: In most Indian states 108 calls an ambulance, and 112 is the national emergency number. Check what works where you live. 1098 is Childline for a child in danger.
flow.context: This is the first step of Our Emergency Card. Here you write the emergency numbers and your address on a card.

flow.do: 1. Heart attack: heavy chest pain that spreads to the arm or jaw, with sweating. 2. Stroke: face droops, one arm is weak, speech is unclear, all of a sudden. 3. Dehydration: dry mouth, sunken eyes, very little urine. 4. Write each on the card with the action: call 108 now, or give ORS in sips.
flow.say: A stroke comes suddenly. Look at the face, the arms and the speech. If any one is wrong, call 108 at once. Every minute counts.
flow.kid: Write the warning signs on the card. For a heart attack or stroke, call 108 now. For dehydration, give ORS in sips. ORS is a salt and sugar drink mixed in clean water.

ask.q: Why does time matter so much in a heart attack or a stroke?
good: The part of the body beyond the blocked artery gets no oxygen.
Its cells begin to die within minutes.

flow.parent: Add the dog bite rule: wash the bite with soap and running water for 15 minutes, then see a doctor the same day. A fever of more than two days, or a cough of more than two weeks, needs a test.
flow.context: In this step of Our Emergency Card you add the warning signs of a heart attack, a stroke and dehydration, and what to do for each.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up plays the operator. 2. Your child calls. 3. They say their name, the address, who is ill and what happened, in four short sentences. 4. Swap roles once.
flow.say: You are the operator. Say: Hello, this is the ambulance. What is your emergency? Then listen to the whole answer.
flow.kid: Pretend to call 108. Say your name. Say where you are. Say who is ill and what happened.

check.q: A grown-up's face droops, one arm is weak and speech is slurred, all of a sudden. What do you do first?
options: Call 108 at once
Wait to see if it passes
Give the person a drink of water
check.why: These are the signs of a stroke, which is a blocked or burst artery in the brain. Every minute without help harms more brain cells. Picking 'wait' is the most common mistake, because the signs may ease for a short time.

flow.context: This is the last step of Our Emergency Card. Here you practise a call to 108, saying who you are, where you are, who is ill and what happened.

activities.title: The Clinic Register: which chart shows a catching illness?
activities.context: In this activity you draw one bar chart from made-up clinic records and read two more sets of numbers. You work out which chart fits an illness that spreads, and which fits an illness that does not.

materials.item: squared paper
a pencil and a ruler
coloured pencils

schedule.what: Draw three bar charts from the clinic numbers. Say what shape each chart has, and which illness each chart could be.

activities.record: Keep your chart X beside the numbers for Y and Z. For each, write its shape in two words, and your guess for the illness. Then write one sentence on what a chart cannot tell you.

setup.art: A page of numbers in a clinic register for fourteen days, in a column headed Fever, next to a bar chart outline.
setup.caption: 1. Read the made-up numbers for Chart X.

setup.art: Three bar charts side by side on squared paper: one rising and falling, one flat and one rising and falling over weeks.
setup.caption: 2. Draw a bar for each number of chart X. Show the shape of Y and Z with your hand.

setup.art: A child tracing the shape of the first chart with a finger and a question mark above it.
setup.caption: 3. Say what shape each chart has, and what that could mean.

flow.do: 1. Chart X is children absent with fever at one school, on days 1 to 14: 1, 1, 3, 5, 9, 14, 16, 12, 8, 4, 2, 1, 1, 0. 2. Chart Y is new asthma visits at one clinic, on days 1 to 14: 4, 3, 5, 4, 6, 4, 3, 5, 4, 5, 3, 4, 5, 4. 3. Chart Z is new dengue cases in one city, in weeks 1 to 10: 2, 3, 6, 12, 25, 40, 48, 30, 15, 6.
flow.say: A clinic writes down its numbers each day. Here are three sets. We will draw each as a chart, and then ask what each shape could mean.
flow.kid: Read the three sets of numbers. Chart X is a school. Chart Y is a clinic. Chart Z is a city.
flow.parent: Take the numbers one set at a time. Draw each chart with its own title. All numbers are made up, to show shapes.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Clinic Register. Here you read three made-up sets of clinic numbers: a school, a clinic and a city.

flow.do: 1. Draw chart X on squared paper. 2. Write the days along the bottom. 3. Colour the tallest bar red. 4. For charts Y and Z, run a finger along the numbers and show the shape with your hand: up, down or flat.
flow.say: Draw a bar for each number of chart X. Then look at the numbers of Y and Z. Which chart goes up and then down? Which one stays about the same?
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each number of chart X. Colour the tallest bar red. Run your finger along Y and Z and show the shape with your hand.

ask.q: Which chart stays about the same from day to day?
good: Chart Y, the asthma visits.

flow.context: In this step of the Clinic Register you draw three bar charts from the clinic numbers and colour the tallest bar of each.

flow.do: 1. Ask what shape chart X has. 2. Ask why a catching illness climbs fast and then falls. 3. Ask what could keep chart Y steady. 4. Ask what chart Z cannot tell you about how dengue spreads.
flow.say: Chart X climbs, peaks and falls. Why would a catching illness do that? Chart Y stays flat. What could cause that? What can chart Z not tell us?
flow.kid: Say the shape of each chart in two words. What could each shape mean?

ask.q: Why does a catching illness first climb and then fall?
good: Each ill person passes it on, so cases grow.
Later, fewer people are left who can catch it, or people take protection.

ask.q: Charts X and Z have the same shape. Does that show that both pass from person to person?
good: No. Dengue passes by mosquito bites.
A chart shows that many cases are linked. It does not show the road.

check.q: A clinic sees about 4 new patients with the same illness every day for two weeks. Which is most likely?
options: A catching illness that is spreading fast
An illness that is not catching, or one steady shared cause
A disease that has just started
check.why: A catching illness grows from day to day. A flat chart suggests a steady cause, such as a long-term illness, or one shared source such as a well. Picking the first option expects every outbreak to climb.

flow.parent: Chart X fits flu. Chart Y fits a not-catching illness such as asthma. Chart Z fits dengue after the monsoon. The shape tells you that cases are joined, and not which road joins them.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Clinic Register. Here you say what each chart's shape means and what a chart cannot tell you.

activities.title: Fact or Fear? Answer back kindly
activities.context: In this activity a grown-up reads six claims that people sometimes make about illness. You say whether each is true, and you practise answering a false claim with facts and kindness.

materials.item: a notebook page and a pencil
a grown-up to read the claims

schedule.what: Answer six claims with true or false. Write a kind reply to two false ones.

activities.record: Write the numbers 1 to 6 and your answer beside each. For two false claims, write a two-sentence reply. The first sentence gives the fact, and the second is kind.

setup.art: A parent reading from a card while a child listens with a pencil, with the number 1 written on a notebook page.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up reads a claim. Say true or false.

setup.art: A notebook page with two replies written, each of two short sentences.
setup.caption: 2. For two false claims, write a two-sentence reply.

setup.art: Two children in school uniform sitting side by side on a bench, sharing a tiffin box.
setup.caption: 3. Read your reply aloud, as if to a classmate.

flow.do: 1. Read each claim and wait for true or false. 2. Claim 1: You can catch HIV from a hug. 3. Claim 2: Cancer is catching. 4. Claim 3: A person with diabetes should eat apart from the family. 5. Claim 4: Once all the blisters of chickenpox have dried into scabs, the person is safe to sit beside. 6. Claim 5: A mosquito who bit a person with HIV can pass HIV to you. 7. Claim 6: A person with TB must stay away from everyone for ever.
flow.say: I will read six claims. Say true or false for each. Then we will talk about why people believe the false ones.
flow.kid: A grown-up reads six claims. Say true or false for each one.
flow.parent: True: claim 4. False: claims 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6. Claim 2 has a twist. A few cancers are started by a germ, such as HPV, but the cancer itself is never catching. For claim 6, a person soon becomes much less likely to pass on TB once medicine begins. They must keep taking every dose.
flow.context: This is the first step of Fact or Fear. Here a grown-up reads six claims about illness and you say whether each is true or false.

flow.do: 1. Your child picks two false claims. 2. They write a reply of two short sentences. 3. The first sentence gives the fact. 4. The second is kind to the person who has the illness.
flow.say: Pick two false claims. Say or write what you would say to a friend who believes one. First say the fact. Then say something kind to the person who has the illness.
flow.kid: Pick two false claims. For each, say or write two sentences. First the fact. Then something kind.

ask.q: Why do people fear an illness before they know how it travels?
good: They do not know the road, so they fear everything.
Fear is quicker than facts.

flow.parent: A strong reply sounds like this: 'HIV does not pass by hugging. Our classmate is just like us, and I want to sit with her.' Praise the fact and the kindness.
flow.context: In this step of Fact or Fear you write a reply to two false claims. Each reply gives the fact first and then says something kind.

flow.do: 1. Read one reply aloud. 2. Ask what the person who has the illness would feel on hearing it.
flow.say: Read one reply aloud. Think of the person who has the illness, listening. How would they feel?
flow.kid: Read one reply aloud. How would the ill person feel on hearing it?

check.q: A classmate has HIV. Which is true and kind?
options: Sit apart, in case you catch it
Play and share a meal, since touch and food do not spread it
Stop talking to her, to be safe
check.why: HIV passes only by infected blood, a few other body fluids and from mother to baby, never by touch, food or toilets. Keeping away from her protects nobody and hurts her. Picking the first option copies a fear and not the facts.

flow.context: This is the last step of Fact or Fear. Here you read your reply aloud and choose the true and kind answer to a classmate's illness.

projects.title: Ten Grown-Ups, Three Questions: which illnesses do people remember?
projects.context: In this five-day project you ask ten grown-ups three questions about illness. You sort their answers into catching and not catching, and write a one-page report.

materials.item: a notebook for the answers
a pencil, a ruler and coloured pencils
ten grown-ups who are happy to answer, from family, neighbours or school

projects.safety: A grown-up goes with you when you ask neighbours. Ask only people who agree. Write no names. Do not ask about private matters such as HIV. Any person may skip a question.

schedule.what: Write your three questions and your guess. Ask the first two grown-ups.
Ask three more grown-ups and write the answers.
Ask the last five grown-ups and write the answers.
Sort all the answers into catching and not catching. Count each road and cause.
Draw a bar chart and write your one-page report.

projects.record: Your report has five parts on one page: my question, my guess, my results chart, what I found, and what I would ask next. Show one bar for each road or cause, drawn or made with counters.

setup.art: A child with a notebook and a pencil asking a neighbour questions at the door, with a parent standing beside her.
setup.caption: 1. Ask ten grown-ups the three questions. Write no names.

setup.art: A notebook page with a tally table: air, water and food, insects, touch, no germ, with small tally marks beside each.
setup.caption: 2. Sort each answer into a road or cause.

setup.art: A bar chart of five bars next to a one-page report with a title.
setup.caption: 3. Draw a bar chart and write your report.

flow.do: 1. Write the questions. Question 1: What illness do you remember most from the last year? Question 2: Did anyone else at home fall ill with it? Question 3: Does anyone in your home have an illness that has lasted for years? 2. Write your guess: which road or cause will come up most, and why?
flow.say: We will ask ten grown-ups three questions about illness. Which kind of illness do you think they will name most? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Write the three questions. Then guess which kind of illness will come up most. Write why.

ask.q: Why must we write no names?
good: People's health is private.
We only need the illnesses, not who had them.

flow.parent: Many children guess that the long illnesses such as diabetes will come up most, since those cause the most deaths. Write the guess down. Do not correct it.
flow.context: This is the first step of Ten Grown-Ups, Three Questions. Here you write your questions and your guess about which kind of illness will come up most.

flow.do: 1. Ask ten grown-ups the three questions over three days. 2. Write each answer in a short line with no names. 3. Thank each person. 4. A grown-up goes with you.
flow.say: Say hello and ask if the person has two minutes. Ask the three questions. Write the answer in a short line. Thank each person.
flow.kid: Ask ten grown-ups the three questions. Write each answer in one short line. Say thank you.
flow.parent: If a person says 'none' or skips a question, write that. Do not press. Ten answers is enough. Five from family and five from neighbours is a good mix.
flow.context: In this step of Ten Grown-Ups, Three Questions you ask ten grown-ups your three questions and write down each answer.

flow.do: 1. Draw a table with the headings: air, water and food, insects, touch, blood, no germ. 2. Put one tally mark for each answer. 3. Count the catching answers and the not-catching answers. 4. Count how many people named a long-term illness.
flow.say: Put each answer under a road or under no germ. Which road has the most marks? How many long illnesses did people name?
flow.kid: Make a table of the six roads and causes. Put a tally mark for each answer. Count the marks.

ask.q: Which came up most: a catching illness or a not-catching one?
good: Usually a catching illness, because colds and fevers are common.

check.q: Most people remember colds and fevers. Yet non-infectious diseases cause six in ten deaths in India. Why can both be true?
options: Colds are common but rarely kill, and long illnesses last for years
The survey is wrong
Colds cause most deaths
check.why: People catch many short illnesses, so they remember them. Heart disease, stroke, diabetes and cancer are fewer but last long and cause more deaths. Picking the second option forgets that a small survey of what people remember measures something different.

flow.context: In this step of Ten Grown-Ups, Three Questions you sort the answers into roads and causes and count each one.

flow.do: 1. Make a bar chart with one bar for each road or cause. Draw it, or stack one counter for each answer. 2. Write a one-page report with five parts: question, guess, chart, what I found, what to ask next. 3. Say if your guess was right and what surprised you.
flow.say: Draw one bar for each road or cause. Then write your report. Was your guess right? What surprised you? What would you ask next?
flow.kid: Make your bar chart. Write your report in five short parts.

ask.q: Ten people is a small sample. What could you do to trust the result more?
good: Ask many more people, from different places and ages.
Ask people in other towns too.

flow.parent: A strong report says what the chart shows and what it cannot show. Ten people from one place cannot tell you about all of India. It is a start.
flow.context: This is the last step of Ten Grown-Ups, Three Questions. Here you draw a bar chart of your results and write a one-page report.

challenges.title: The Waiting Room: where should eight people sit?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about fresh air. You plan where eight people should sit in a small clinic waiting room, where one person has a cough.
challenges.problem: A small clinic has a waiting room that is 4 metres long and 3 metres wide. It has one door on a short wall and one window on the opposite wall. It has a ceiling fan and no air conditioner. Eight people wait at once, and one has a cough. Plan where each person sits, and which openings stay open, so that the germs in the cough reach as few people as possible.
constraints: The room has only one door and one window. No new windows may be added.
Every seat is at least 1 metre from the next.
The person with the cough must still be able to reach the doctor's door.
You must show which way the air moves, using something you tested.
materials: squared paper, where one square stands for 50 centimetres
strips of tissue paper, 2 centimetres wide and 15 centimetres long, taped to a pencil as a streamer
eight coins or buttons, and a small piece of red paper
a room at home with a door and a window on different walls
a ceiling fan or table fan
general: Open the window and the door, so that the air flows through the room.
Seat people in a line across the room, away from the straight path between the door and the window.
Put the person with the cough near the opening where the air leaves, so the air carries the cough out.
Ask people to wait outside when the room is full.
creative: Put a table fan in the window, blowing outward. It pulls the old air out and lets fresh air in at the door.
Give appointments at fixed times, so fewer people wait together.
Put chairs in a shaded passage outside, where there is more moving air than inside.
Mark the seats with tape on the floor, so everyone keeps 1 metre apart.
challenges.your_turn: Now draw the room on squared paper. Show the door, the window and the fan. Use coins for the eight seats, with a red mark on the person with the cough. Add paper arrows for the air. Ask a grown-up to check it, and to say what they would change.

setup.art: A child holding a tissue-paper streamer on a pencil near an open window in a room, the streamer blowing sideways.
setup.caption: 1. Test the air in a room at home with a streamer.

setup.art: A floor plan on squared paper, 8 squares by 6 squares, with a door on one short wall and a window on the opposite wall.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the waiting room on squared paper.

setup.art: The same plan with eight small circles for seats, one marked red near the window, and curved arrows between door and window.
setup.caption: 3. Mark the seats, the person with the cough and the air arrows.

flow.do: 1. Read the problem aloud. 2. Ask which seats would be worst. 3. Ask why.
flow.say: Eight people wait in a small room, and one person has a cough. Where would you not want to sit? Why?
flow.kid: Read the problem. Which seats are worst? Say why.

ask.q: Why is a closed room worse than one with open windows?
good: The fine particles from a cough stay in the room.
With no fresh air coming in, they build up.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Waiting Room challenge. Here you read the problem and think about which seats would be worst.

flow.do: 1. In a room at home, open the door and the window on different walls. 2. Hold the streamer in the middle, near the window and near the door. 3. At each place, lay a paper strip as an arrow pointing the way it blows. 4. Then shut the window and repeat. 5. Then turn on the fan and repeat.
flow.say: Hold the streamer still in the middle of the room. Which way does it move? Do it near the window, and near the door. At each place, lay down a paper strip to point the way it moves.
flow.kid: Hold the streamer in the middle, then at the window, then at the door. Lay a paper strip at each place, pointing the way it blows.

ask.q: What happens to the streamer when the window is shut?
good: It hangs still or hardly moves.
The air in the room does not flow.

flow.parent: The air may move in the opposite direction on another day, since the wind changes. Check the streamer each time. With both openings open, the streamer should move steadily from one side to the other.
flow.context: In this step of the Waiting Room challenge you test how the air moves in a room at home, using a tissue-paper streamer.

flow.do: 1. Draw the room on squared paper, 8 squares by 6. 2. Mark the door and window. 3. Put your paper strips on the plan where they blew. 4. Put eight coins on the plan as seats, at least 2 squares apart. 5. Put a small piece of red paper on the coin for the person with the cough.
flow.say: Now make your plan. Where does the air go? Where should the person with the cough sit? Who sits where the air is freshest?
flow.kid: Draw the room. Put your paper strips on it. Put eight coins down as seats. Mark the person with the cough in red.
flow.parent: Good plans seat the person with the cough near the opening where the air leaves. They are not upwind of the others. Seats a metre apart also help.
flow.context: In this step of the Waiting Room challenge you draw a plan of the room with the air arrows and eight seats.

flow.do: 1. Show the plan to a grown-up. 2. Ask what they would change. 3. Write one thing you would change.
flow.say: Show your plan to a grown-up. Explain where the air goes and why each person sits where they do. Then ask what they would change.
flow.kid: Show your plan to a grown-up. Explain it. Write one thing you would change.

check.q: With a door and a window open on opposite walls, where should the person with the cough sit?
options: Near the opening where the air leaves the room
Near the opening where fresh air comes in
In the middle, away from both
check.why: Air carries the fine particles of a cough along with it. If the person sits where the air leaves, the cough is carried straight out. If she sits where fresh air enters, the air carries her cough across everyone else. Picking the middle leaves her breath to mix with the whole room.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Waiting Room challenge. Here you show your plan to a grown-up and explain where the person with the cough sits.

challenges.title: The Camp Plan: three days in a forest with thirty children
challenges.context: This is a planning challenge about staying well. You plan the health protections for a school camp of three days in a forest in Karnataka.
challenges.problem: Thirty children and four teachers camp for three days in a forest near the Western Ghats in Karnataka. There is a stream, a camp kitchen, tents with open flaps, ticks and mosquitoes. The nearest hospital is 40 kilometres away. Plan how the camp stays well. Cover at least four of the five roads that germs travel.
constraints: Cover at least four of the five roads: air, water and food, insects and ticks, touch, blood.
For each road, name the protection and say how often it is done.
The plan must say what happens if a child gets a fever or loose motions.
Teachers may give ORS but not an antibiotic or any other medicine without a doctor.
Everything must fit in one page.
materials: your notes on the five roads and the shields
a grown-up who has been to a camp, to ask
general: Boil or filter all drinking water, and keep it covered.
Wash hands with soap before every meal and after the toilet.
