worksheets.title: Two kinds of disease, five roads and their shields

items.p: Which of these diseases is caused by a germ?
items.why: Typhoid is caused by a bacterium who travels in water and food. Diabetes, anaemia and asthma begin inside the body, and no germ causes them.

items.p: Sort these diseases into infectious and non-infectious.
items.why: Cholera, measles and malaria are each caused by a germ. A heart attack comes from a blocked artery, anaemia from too little iron, and diabetes from sugar that stays in the blood. No germ causes those three.

items.p: A disease that passes straight from one person to another is called ____.
a: contagious
items.why: Contagious means passing from person to person. Every contagious disease is infectious, but malaria is infectious and not contagious, because a mosquito must carry the germ.

items.p: Match each road to a disease that travels by it.
items.why: Tuberculosis germs ride in the breath of an ill person. Typhoid germs reach water and food from stools. Dengue needs an Aedes mosquito. Ringworm passes by skin and shared towels. Hepatitis B passes by blood.

items.p: You can catch malaria by sitting beside a person who has malaria.
items.why: False. A malaria parasite must be carried by a female Anopheles mosquito. A person with malaria is safe to sit beside. A net and no standing water protect the family.

items.p: Which protection blocks the mosquito road?
items.why: A net keeps the mosquito from biting. A mask works on the air road, boiled water on the water road, and hand washing on the touch road.

items.p: Put these in order, from first to last, for an infectious disease.
items: The germ gets into the body
The person gets better or is treated
The germ multiplies while the person feels well
a: The germ gets into the body
The germ multiplies while the person feels well
The first symptom appears
The person gets better or is treated
items.why: The germ gets in and multiplies for days before anything is felt. That gap is the incubation period. Then the first symptom appears, and the person recovers or is treated.

items.p: An antibiotic cures a cold.
items.why: False. A virus causes a cold, and antibiotics kill bacteria only. Rest and drinks help while the body deals with the virus.

items.p: Which of these diseases does a mosquito net not protect against?
items.why: Cholera travels by water and food, so a net does nothing against it. Malaria and filariasis are both carried by mosquitoes.

items.p: Too little iron in the food causes ____.
a: anaemia
items.why: Iron is needed to make red blood cells. Too little leaves a person tired and pale. It is a deficiency disease, and no germ causes it.

items.p: Boiling water protects against cholera but not against diabetes. Explain why.
items.a: Cholera is caused by a germ who travels in dirty water, and boiling kills the germ. Diabetes has no germ in the water behind it. It comes from the body's use of sugar, so a different shield is needed.
items.why: A strong answer says that the protection must match the road or the cause.

items.p: On a map of a catching illness, which ill houses stand beside an earlier ill house?
items.why: On the catching map of the Two Maps Test, a house could fall ill only from an ill neighbour. So every ill house except the first had an earlier ill neighbour. On the not-catching map only some did, by chance.

items.p: Label the five roads that germs travel, with one disease for each.
a: Air: for example tuberculosis
Water and food: for example typhoid
Insects and ticks: for example malaria
Touch: for example ringworm
Blood and body fluids: for example hepatitis B
items.why: Any true disease for each road is a good answer. The roads decide the protection, so naming them is the first step of stopping a disease.
items.art: A blank outline of a child with five empty label lines around it and a small arrow pointing at the nose, mouth, skin, a mosquito and a drop of blood.

items.p: Six children in one class have a fever and a cough. What should the school do?

views.says: Send the whole class home for a week, to be safe.
Send the ill children home and open the windows. A child who coughs for more than two weeks should be tested.
It is only a cold. Nothing needs to change.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from what you have learned. Then answer back one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. The doctor's view fits the air road: fresh air thins the germs, ill children stay home, and a long cough may be TB. Sending healthy children home helps little. Doing nothing ignores that a cough spreads germs.
items.why: Strong answers use the road the germ travels, and do not just say the first thing that comes to mind.

items.p: Draw a child with a cough. Show two ways to stop the germs reaching the next person.
items.a: A child coughing into an elbow or a cloth, with a window open behind, or a mask on the child. Two clear labels, such as covered cough and fresh air.
items.why: A strong drawing shows two real shields on the air road and labels each one.
items.art: A blank page with a faint outline of a child standing near a window.

items.p: What does a risk factor do?
opts: Raises the chance of a disease
items.why: A risk factor changes how many people in a group fall ill. It does not decide what happens to any one person. Picking 'decides who falls ill' is the most common mistake.

items.p: A man smoked all his life and stayed well until he was 90. So tobacco is not a risk.
items.why: False. In the tobacco group of the Risk Dice Test, about half the people stayed well, and tobacco still tripled the number who fell ill. One person's story cannot show what a risk does.

items.p: What causes a heart attack?
opts: A blocked artery of the heart
items.why: A fatty layer narrows an artery, and a clot can block it. The heart muscle beyond the block gets no oxygen. Germs and cold weather are not the cause.

items.p: Sort these diseases by their main cause.
items.why: Sickle cell disease comes through the genes. Goitre comes from too little iodine. Fluorosis comes from too much fluoride in water. Type 2 diabetes builds up slowly with age, weight, little movement and genes.

items.p: Each group has 30 people. 5 fall ill without tobacco and 15 with tobacco. How many times as many is that?
items.why: 15 divided by 5 is 3. Three times as many fell ill in the tobacco group, and yet half of that group stayed well.

items.p: Three of these are non-infectious. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: Tuberculosis is caused by a bacterium who passes through the air. Diabetes, asthma and anaemia are non-infectious.

items.p: On a map, no ill house stands beside an earlier ill house. What does this suggest?
opts: The illness does not pass from person to person
items.why: A catching illness leaves chains, with each new ill house beside an earlier one. Scattered houses suggest the cases are not linked by contact. Mosquito diseases can look like this too, so the next step is to find what the ill people share.

items.p: Put these steps in order for finding out whether a disease is catching.
items: Remove the shared thing and watch the cases
Mark the ill houses on a map
Find the germ in the ill people
Look for what the ill people share
a: Mark the ill houses on a map
Look for what the ill people share
Remove the shared thing and watch the cases
Find the germ in the ill people
items.why: A map shows the pattern. Looking for what the ill share gives a suspect. Removing the suspect and watching the cases is a test. Finding the germ in the ill people confirms the cause.

items.p: Many ill people living around one well proves that the illness is catching.
items.why: False. A cluster shows only that the ill people share something. It may be the water in the well, which is not catching from person to person. The next step is to test what they share.

items.p: A child sits beside a classmate who has HIV. Which of these is safe?
opts: Sharing a bandage with blood on it
items.why: HIV does not pass by food, touch, toilets or mosquitoes. It passes by infected blood, a few body fluids and from mother to baby. A used needle or a bloody bandage can carry blood.

items.p: The time between a germ getting into the body and the first symptom is the ____ period.
a: incubation
items.why: During the incubation period the germ multiplies while the person feels well. Chickenpox has 10 to 21 days, and flu has 1 to 4 days.

items.p: Explain why a person with no symptoms can still pass a germ to someone else.
items.a: A germ can be in the body and multiplying before any symptom shows. Some people are carriers, who carry the germ for a long time and feel well. Their breath, hands or food can still pass the germ on.
items.why: A strong answer names the incubation period or a carrier.

items.p: Why can a map of many cases show something that one ill person alone cannot?
items.a: One ill person looks the same whether the illness is catching or not. Only many cases together show a pattern, such as chains of houses, a growing number each day, or a cluster around one shared thing.
items.why: A strong answer says that 'catching' is a fact about how cases are joined, and one case alone has no links to see.

items.p: A neighbour has TB and has started medicine. Should the family stay away?

views.says: Stay away until the cough has gone completely.
After the first weeks of medicine, a person is much less likely to pass on TB. Keep the windows open and make sure every dose is taken.
Please do not leave me alone. I need food and company to get better.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from what you have learned. Then answer back one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. The nurse's view fits what is known: TB travels on the air road, so fresh air and treatment block it, and staying away from a person who is on treatment does little. The person with TB needs care. Fear is understandable, but facts show what helps.
items.why: Strong answers use the air road and the fact that medicine lowers the chance of spreading.

items.p: Label the three parts of this artery.
a: Part A: a fatty layer on the wall
Part B: a clot
Part C: the space left for blood
items.why: A fatty layer narrows the tube. A clot on the layer can block the space that is left for blood. The part of the body beyond the block gets no oxygen.
items.art: A cut-away artery with a yellow fatty layer on one wall, a dark clot on the layer and a narrow gap for blood, each marked with a blank arrow.

worksheets.title: Telling them apart, arguing and planning

items.p: Many ill people live around one well, and the nurses who care for them stay well. What is the best next step?
opts: Find what the ill share, and test the well
Send everyone out of the village
items.why: A cluster and well nurses suggest a shared cause and not person-to-person spread. The next step is to test what they share and see if the cases stop when it is removed.

items.p: Which fact is the best evidence that a disease does not pass from person to person?
opts: Nurses who care for patients every day stay well
Many patients live in one town
items.why: If the disease passed from person to person, the nurses would fall ill. Dr Goldberger used this clue for pellagra. Many patients in one town, or feeling very ill, tell us nothing about the road.

items.p: A catching illness spreads through a school. Why do the daily cases first climb fast?
opts: Each ill child passes it on to more children
The germ gets stronger each day
items.why: Each ill child can pass the germ to several others, so the number grows each day. It slows when fewer children are left to catch it, or when people take protection.

items.p: One sickle cell gene protects against malaria. Why is the gene common where malaria has been common?
opts: Carriers of one copy survived malaria more often
items.why: People with one copy are well and are less likely to die of malaria. So they had more children, and the gene stayed common. People with two copies have a serious disease.

items.p: Stomach ulcers are caused by worry and spicy food, and by nothing else.
items.why: False. Barry Marshall and Robin Warren showed in the 1980s that a bacterium causes most stomach ulcers. Antibiotics cure them.

items.p: A vaccine protects only the person who gets it.
items.why: False. A vaccinated person cannot pass the germ on, so the chain stops at that person. This protects people around them, such as babies who are too young for the vaccine.

items.p: Match each cause to a disease it can lead to.
pairs: A virus who stays for years
items.why: Iodine is needed to make a hormone, and too little swells the neck. Tobacco damages the cells of the mouth. Sickle cell disease is inherited. Standing water breeds Aedes mosquitoes. The HPV virus starts most cancers of the cervix.

items.p: Suppose 20 of 400 non-smokers and 80 of 400 smokers get lung disease. How many times as likely are smokers?
items.why: Smokers: 80 out of 400, which is 1 in 5. Non-smokers: 20 out of 400, which is 1 in 20. One in 5 is 4 times 1 in 20.

items.p: A mosquito who carries a germ from one person to the next is called a ____.
a: vector
items.why: A vector is an animal who carries a germ between people. Female Anopheles mosquitoes are the vectors of malaria, and female Aedes mosquitoes of dengue.

items.p: Soap and water help against cholera but not against malaria. Explain why.
items.a: Cholera germs travel on hands, food and water, so clean hands block part of that road. Malaria germs travel inside a mosquito and enter by her bite. Soap does nothing to the mosquito's bite.
items.why: A strong answer matches the protection to the road.

items.p: In groups of 6, tobacco did not always look worse. What does this say about how many people a study needs?
items.a: With few people, luck can hide the real difference between the groups. With many people, luck evens out and the real effect shows. So a health study needs hundreds or thousands of people.
items.why: A strong answer says that chance matters most in small groups.

items.p: Some scientists think children need to meet harmless microbes early in life. What evidence would support this idea?
items.a: Children who grow up on farms or with older brothers and sisters would need to have less allergy and asthma. The pattern should also hold after other causes, such as dirty air, are taken into account.
items.why: A strong answer asks for a pattern across many children and for other causes to be ruled out.

items.p: Is it fair to say that a person with a lifestyle disease caused it themselves?

views.says: Tobacco and little movement raise the chance, so changing them helps. But genes, age, dirty air and money matter too.

views.who: A person with lung cancer who never smoked
views.says: I did everything right and still fell ill. Blame does not help me.

views.who: A person who has chewed tobacco for years
views.says: I started young, when friends offered it and the shop sold it to me. It is hard to stop.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from what you have learned. Then answer back one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. A risk raises the chance for a group and does not decide for one person. Many causes add up, and some cannot be changed. So a risk is a reason to change what can be changed, and not a reason to blame a person who is ill.
items.why: Strong answers use the idea that a risk raises the chance but does not decide.

items.p: Draw a map of nine houses with an illness that is not catching. Put all the ill houses around one well.
items.a: A grid of nine houses with a well marked in the middle. The ill houses are the ones closest to the well, and they are not joined in a chain of earlier and later cases.
items.why: A strong drawing shows a cluster around one shared thing, marked as the well, and not a chain from house to house.
items.art: A blank grid of three rows and three columns of small houses.

items.p: Which of these would lower the chance of a heart attack?
items.why: A heart attack comes from a blocked artery, and movement, no tobacco and less salt and fried food lower the chance. A net and boiled water protect against infections.

opts: An animal who carries a germ between people
quiz.why: A vector carries a germ from one person to the next. A female Anopheles mosquito is the vector of malaria. A medicine is not a vector, and a fever is a symptom.

quiz.p: Which disease passes through the air?
quiz.why: Tuberculosis germs ride in droplets and aerosols from a cough. Cholera travels by water and food, and dengue by an Aedes mosquito.

quiz.p: How does dengue reach a new person?
quiz.why: A female Aedes mosquito carries the dengue virus and passes it on when she bites. A person with dengue is safe to sit beside.
Typhoid travels by water and food. Boiling water and washing hands block that road. A net blocks mosquitoes, and an open window thins germs in the air.

quiz.p: Hugging a person who has HIV can pass the virus on.
quiz.why: False. HIV passes only by infected blood, a few other body fluids and from mother to baby. Hugging, shared food and toilets do not pass it on.

quiz.p: Which of these diseases is non-infectious?
quiz.why: Asthma is the airways reacting to smoke, dust or pollen, and no germ causes it. Measles and chickenpox are caused by viruses.

opts: An artery in the brain is blocked or bursts
A germ enters the brain through water
quiz.why: Brain cells beyond a blocked or burst artery get no oxygen and begin to die within minutes. This is why a stroke is an emergency.

quiz.p: In diabetes, what stays too high in the blood?
quiz.why: Insulin lets sugar pass from the blood into the cells. In diabetes there is too little insulin, or the cells do not respond to it, so sugar stays in the blood.

quiz.p: Cancer passes from one person to another by touch.
quiz.why: False. Cancer begins in a person's own cells. A few cancers are started by a germ, such as HPV, but the cancer itself is not catching.

quiz.p: Which pattern on a map suggests a catching illness?
opts: Each new ill house is beside an earlier ill house
Ill houses are all in one colour
quiz.why: A catching illness passes from house to house, so new cases appear beside earlier ones and form chains. An even spread or one colour says nothing about chains.

quiz.p: Two groups of 30 people have 5 and 15 ill people. What does this show about the second group?
opts: The risk is higher, but not everyone fell ill
quiz.why: Three times as many fell ill, so the chance was higher. But half the group stayed well, so the risk did not decide who fell ill.

quiz.p: Which of these is something scientists still argue about?
opts: Whether too little early contact with microbes raises allergies
quiz.why: The hygiene hypothesis is still being tested. Hand washing and the mosquito road of malaria are settled facts.

open_questions.q: Does meeting more microbes early in life protect children from allergies and asthma?
open_questions.why_open: Children on farms have less asthma, but many other things differ between farms and cities. Nobody has yet separated the causes.

open_questions.q: Why do some people infected with the same germ stay well while others become very ill?
open_questions.why_open: Age, genes, food and earlier infections all matter. Nobody can yet predict who will become very ill.

open_questions.q: How many long-term diseases, such as heart disease and some cancers, have a germ among their causes?
open_questions.why_open: A few do, such as HPV and the stomach bacterium. Scientists are testing others, and for most the evidence is still weak.

open_questions.q: Can a vaccine give full and lasting protection against malaria?
open_questions.why_open: Two malaria vaccines are now in use. Both give only partial protection, and the malaria parasite changes her coat in the body.

open_questions.q: Can the habits of friends spread from person to person, somewhat as germs do?
open_questions.why_open: Some studies say yes. Others found the same 'spread' for height and headaches, so the method may be misleading.

maths.problem: In the Risk Dice Test, 5 of 30 people without tobacco fell ill, and 15 of 30 with tobacco. Write each as a fraction in its simplest form and as a percentage.
maths.answer: 1 in 6, about 17 percent, and 1 in 2, which is 50 percent.
maths.explain: 5 out of 30 is 1 out of 6, because both numbers divide by 5. 1 divided by 6 is about 0.17, which is 17 percent. 15 out of 30 is 1 out of 2, which is 50 percent. The risk is about 3 times as high.
maths.context: This is about the Risk Dice Test. In it, two groups of 30 people roll dice to find who falls ill, with and without tobacco.
maths.why_maths: Fractions and percentages let us compare two groups of the same size, or of different sizes, fairly.

maths.problem: In the Risk Dice Test, a person in the tobacco group falls ill on a roll of 1, 2 or 3. What fraction of rolls make a person ill? In a group of 600 people, about how many fall ill?
maths.answer: 3 out of 6, which is 1 half. About 300 people.
maths.explain: The numbers 1, 2 and 3 are 3 of the 6 faces on the die, so the chance is 3 out of 6, or 1 half. Half of 600 is 300. In real life the number will be near 300, and not exactly 300.
maths.context: This is about the Risk Dice Test. In it, a die stands for chance in a group of people who use tobacco.
maths.why_maths: A chance for one person gives a good guess for a large group, even though nobody can say who will fall ill.

maths.problem: In a made-up pair of maps for the Two Maps Test, both maps had 14 ill houses. The catching map took 4 days. The not-catching map took 8 days. How many ill houses a day was that on each map, on average? Why does the catching map go faster?
maths.answer: 3.5 a day on the catching map and 1.75 a day on the other. On the catching map each ill house makes more ill houses.
maths.explain: 14 divided by 4 is 3.5. 14 divided by 8 is 1.75, which is half as many. On the catching map each new ill house can pass the illness to its neighbours, so the number each day grows. On the other map the die picks two houses a day, whatever the neighbours do.
maths.context: This is about the Two Maps Test. In it, a catching illness and an illness that is not catching are both spread across 36 houses with dice.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the total by the days gives a speed, and a speed lets us compare two maps that took different times.

maths.problem: In a made-up record, four people first felt ill on days 12, 14, 15 and 17 after meeting a visitor with chickenpox. What are the shortest and longest incubation periods? What is the difference?
maths.answer: The shortest is 12 days and the longest is 17 days. The difference is 5 days.
maths.explain: The earliest first-symptom day is 12 and the latest is 17. 17 minus 12 is 5. The usual range for chickenpox is 10 to 21 days, so these numbers fit inside it.
maths.context: This is about the Incubation Detective. In it, three groups of people mark the day on which they first felt ill after meeting an ill visitor.
maths.why_maths: The longest incubation period tells a family how many days to wait before they know a visitor did not pass on the germ.

maths.problem: About 100 million people in India have diabetes, and India has about 1,400 million people. About what fraction of all people is that? About what percentage?
maths.answer: About 1 in 14, which is a little over 7 percent.
maths.explain: 100 out of 1,400 is 1 out of 14, because both numbers divide by 100. 1 divided by 14 is about 0.07, which is 7 percent. These are rounded numbers, so the answer is a rough guide.
maths.context: This is about diabetes, a disease in which sugar stays in the blood. A very large number of people in India live with it.
maths.why_maths: A fraction turns a huge number into something we can picture, such as 1 person in a crowd of 14.

maths.problem: In India, non-infectious diseases caused about 38 in every 100 deaths in 1990 and more than 60 in every 100 in 2016. Did the share double? How much did it rise by?
maths.answer: No. It rose by more than 22 in every 100, which is about 1.6 times as large.
maths.explain: 60 minus 38 is 22, and the real rise is a little more. Double 38 would be 76, which is far more than 60. So the share did not double. 60 divided by 38 is about 1.6.
maths.context: This is about the changing causes of death in India. A large study counted the causes of death in every state in 1990 and in 2016.
maths.why_maths: Checking 'did it double?' stops us from saying a change is bigger than it is.

maths.problem: A mosquito can take about a week to grow from an egg to an adult. A family empties a bucket every 5 days. Another family empties theirs every 9 days. Which family stops mosquitoes from growing in the bucket? Why?
maths.answer: The first family. An egg laid just after emptying has 5 days to grow, which is less than a week, and then the bucket is emptied again.
maths.explain: Eggs can become adults in about a week. If the water is thrown out every 5 days, no egg lasts long enough. If it is thrown out every 9 days, eggs laid just after emptying have 9 days and some grow into adults.
maths.context: This is about dengue and the Aedes mosquito, who lays her eggs in clean standing water in buckets, coolers and tyres.
maths.why_maths: Comparing two time gaps against a growing time tells a family how often they must empty the water.

maths.problem: In a clinic register for flu, the new cases each day were 1, 3, 9 and 27. What pattern is it? If the pattern went on, how many new cases would there be on day 6?
maths.answer: Each day has 3 times as many as the day before. On day 6 there would be 243.
maths.explain: 1 times 3 is 3, and 3 times 3 is 9, and 9 times 3 is 27. Day 5 is 81 and day 6 is 243. Real outbreaks slow down as fewer people are left to catch the illness, so the pattern cannot go on for long.
maths.context: This is about the shape of a catching illness. In the Two Maps Test and the Clinic Register, the number of new cases grows each day at first.
maths.why_maths: A pattern shows how fast cases could grow, and why the first days of an outbreak matter most.

warmup.a: A germ causes an infectious disease. No germ causes a non-infectious disease, and nobody catches it.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people learn to tell an infectious disease from a non-infectious one? This card tells the true story of a disease that almost every doctor put in the wrong group.
how_we_found_out.story: In the early 1900s a disease called pellagra spread across the southern United States. It caused a rough red rash, loose motions and confusion, and thousands died each year. Cases crowded together in orphanages, prisons and poor villages. So most doctors were sure that a germ caused it. In 1914 the government sent Dr Joseph Goldberger to find the germ. He noticed something else. In the orphanages and hospitals, the children and patients got pellagra. The nurses and staff, who touched them every day, never did. The staff ate meat, milk and vegetables. The patients ate mostly maize bread and syrup. Goldberger gave children in two orphanages fresh meat, milk and vegetables, and their pellagra went away. In 1916 he, his wife Mary and other volunteers swallowed capsules of scabs from patients. They also took injections of patients' blood. None of them fell ill. Pellagra was a deficiency disease. In 1937 Conrad Elvehjem found the missing nutrient, a B vitamin now called niacin.
how_we_found_out.who: Joseph Goldberger, a doctor in the United States Public Health Service. Mary Farrar Goldberger, his wife, who volunteered. Conrad Elvehjem, an American chemist.
how_we_found_out.when: Goldberger began in 1914. The volunteer tests were in 1916. Niacin was identified in 1937.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That pellagra was an infectious disease, because the cases crowded together. The cases crowded together because poor people in one place ate the same poor food. Staff who shared the rooms but not the food stayed well, and volunteers who took in material from patients stayed well.
how_we_found_out.art: A doctor in a 1914 suit standing in an orphanage dining hall, looking from the children's plates of maize bread to a nurse's plate of meat and vegetables.

roots.context: We have made two maps with dice and learned how people tell a catching illness from one that is not. Now we ask what this tells us about one person and many people.

deep_truth.truth: In the Two Maps Test, both maps had the same number of ill houses. Any one ill house, looked at alone, could belong to either map. On the catching map, every new ill house stood beside a house that fell ill earlier. So people learn whether an illness is catching by studying many patients together.
deep_truth.habit: We think of an illness as something inside one body, to be found by examining that body. But whether an illness is catching is not found inside one body. It is found by looking at how the cases are connected to each other. This shows in the pattern of who fell ill, where and when. The same is true of a risk. One smoker's life cannot show what tobacco does. The lives of thousands of people can.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Two Maps Test, the two maps have equal numbers of ill houses, and only the pattern differs. In the Risk Dice Test, no single ill person shows whether the risk made them ill, but the two groups of 30 differ clearly. Goldberger found out that pellagra was not infectious by comparing patients with their nurses. If your own maps or groups came out differently, write down what you got and run them again.

three.who_am_i: Your health depends partly on you and partly on the people around you. The water, the air and the vaccines that you share with your town protect you as much as your own habits do.
three.what_is_life: Germs are living beings, and they need a way to reach the next body. People, mosquitoes, ticks and germs all live close together. An illness is one thing that can happen when their lives meet.
three.what_is_this_world: Some facts cannot be seen by looking at one thing alone. They show up only when you look at many things together. The pattern on the map was one example.

roots.thread: A doctor examines one patient, and that is how most of us think about illness. But the two maps showed that some facts are about the connections between people. A catching illness passes from one person to the next. You cannot see that by looking at one ill person. A risk is a difference between two groups. You cannot see that in one person either. So health is something people share, as well as something each person has alone. Clean water, clean air and vaccines work this way: each protects a person by protecting everyone around them.

teachings.teaching: A student asks how one disease can strike a whole town at once, when the people differ in body, food and habits. The teacher answers that they share four things: the air, the water, the place and the season.
teachings.link: This is the reasoning of the Two Maps Test, written down in India roughly two thousand years ago. When many different people fall ill together, look for what they share.

teachings.source: The story of Kisa Gotami, in the commentary on the Dhammapada, verse 114
teachings.teaching: A mother whose child has died asks the Buddha for medicine. He asks her to bring a mustard seed from a house where nobody has ever died. She goes from door to door and finds no such house.
teachings.link: Kisa Gotami learned something about her own loss only by visiting many houses. In this unit too, some truths about one illness appear only when many homes are looked at together.

teachings.source: Hippocrates, On Airs, Waters and Places, opening section
teachings.teaching: A doctor who arrives in a new town should first study its winds, its water, its soil and the way its people live.
teachings.link: The Greek doctors did not know about germs. But they saw that the diseases of a town follow what the whole town breathes, drinks and eats.

science.text: Whether a disease passes from person to person is found by studying the pattern of many cases, and then confirmed by finding the germ.
A vaccinated person protects the people around them, because the germ cannot pass on through that person to the next one.
Some scientists think that habits such as smoking and overeating also spread between friends, somewhat as germs do. Others think the studies were misread.

other_view.who: Many doctors who treat patients one at a time
other_view.view: They would say that a pattern in thousands of people tells little about the one person in front of them. An average says nothing certain about this patient's body or this patient's future. For them, the truth about an illness is found by listening to the ill person and examining them. They warn that people treated as numbers are easily forgotten.

practice.title: The air we share
practice.say: Sit near an open window with someone from your family. Breathe in slowly through your nose, and breathe out slowly. Do this ten times. The air you breathe out mixes into the room. The other person breathes some of that air in. The window carries part of it away to the street. Now sit quietly for one minute. Think of everyone who shares this air, this water and this street with you.
practice.kid: Sit near an open window with someone. Breathe in slowly. Breathe out slowly. Do this ten times. Your breath mixes into the room. The other person breathes some of it. The window carries some away. Sit quietly for one minute. Think of everyone who shares this air.

ask: One ill person looks the same whether the illness is catching or not. So how can anyone find out that an illness is catching? What do they have to look at?
Your own habits protect you, and so do your town's water and air. Which part of your health belongs only to you?
A doctor studies one patient, and a map studies thousands. What does each one see that the other misses?

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game and challenge was reasoned through step by step for a family in a city flat. None has yet been tried at home. So the numbers and times below are expected, and not measured. The Two Maps Test (core) needs only squared paper and a die. Map A reaches 12 or more ill houses in about 4 or 5 days, and about once in 30 maps the illness dies out first, so the step says to start again. Map B takes about 7 to 10 days of rolls, and usually 3 to 9 of its ill houses stand beside an earlier ill house by chance. So one pair of neighbours proves nothing, and the whole pattern is the evidence. The Risk Dice Test (core) needs a die and paper. Expect about 5 ill people in the first group of 30 and about 15 in the second, and anything from 2 to 9 and from 10 to 20 is common. In small groups of 6 the tobacco group comes out no worse in about one round in six, which is the point of the step. The numbers 1 in 6 and 1 in 2 are made up to suit a die, and real risks differ from disease to disease. One Opening or Two needs a clear 1-litre bottle, an agarbatti and a torch. A grown-up lights the stick and does the cutting. The closed bottle should still show haze after 3 minutes. The one-opening bottle thins slowly, and the two-opening bottle should clear in well under a minute with a fan or a moving breeze. In a still room the times may all be longer, and the step says what to do. Smoke is not germs. It stands for the fine particles of a cough, which float and move in the same way. The Waiting Room challenge uses a tissue streamer, and the air may flow the other way on another day. Ten Grown-Ups, Three Questions needs a grown-up to go with the child, and no names are written. The Kyasanur Forest story is made up, but the disease, the dates, the dead monkeys, the ticks and the finding that nurses did not fall ill are real.
